#4724. Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Needs a Killer Cast. Here’s Who Should Join Him.

A great 007 movie isn’t just about the man himself. Now we can start to find the next Bond Girl, villain, and more—and really have some fun.

OUR LONG INTERNATIONAL nightmare is finally over: We have a new James Bond. On Monday, Robert Pattinson was announced as 007, beating out contenders that included Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor. Considering Pattinson is currently double dipping as Bruce Wayne—and the fact that Bond is historically a star-making role, rather than a role for an established star—his casting won’t be everyone’s cup of tea. (My two cents: he would’ve been a god-tier Bond villain.)

Still, it’s hard to deny that Pattinson is going to crush the role. From buzzy indies like The Lighthouse and High Life to blockbusters like Mickey 17 and The Odyssey, he’s long been on a heater. (Nobody using Edward Cullen as a punchline against him is further proof of that.) For Amazon, whose stewardship of the Bond franchise was always going to be met with scrutiny, there’s no shame in making the safe, sensible choice.

But landing on a new 007 is only the beginning. James Bond isn’t just about the title character: The franchise can also be a career-defining move for actors enlisted to play recurring characters (M) and archetypes (the gimmicky henchmen) that bring the world to life. For Pattinson and director Denis Villeneuve, this new Bond entry needs to be populated with the very best supporting players Jeff Bezos’s money can buy.

With that in mind, here’s our dream casting for the seven most important non-Bond roles in the new film.

The Bond franchise has been around for decades, and the films are often a reflection of both the world around them and the current state of moviemaking. The Timothy Dalton era was gritty and grounded as the Cold War wound down; the Daniel Craig movies were serialized in the age of cinematic universes. For a modern-day Bond, then, we should have a villain that feels made for the 2020s. In other words: cast a sinister nerd—and more specifically, cast Samuel Blenkin.

In biopics and documentaries alike, tech bros are cinema’s latest villain du jour. Between the untold economic and environmental damage they've caused in the real world, nobody is going to feel bad about these guys being painted in an unflattering light. In that respect, Blenkin would be a fun casting. If Tenet was a great test run for Pattinson as 007, then Alien: Earth, in which Blenkin plays an impetuous tech bro with the gall to mess around with Xenomorphs (!!!), is proof that he could bring the same (respectfully) punchable energy to Bond. Say what you will about Zack Snyder’s DC movies, but picking the actor who played Mark Zuckerberg to be his Lex Luthor was ahead of the curve. Bond would be wise to meet the moment.

Runner-up: Jensen Huang (with the leather jacket, obviously).

The next M has big shoes to fill. Dame Judi Dench played the character across eight films and two separate Bonds over a period of 20 years, and Ralph Fiennes then made the role his own (as he always does), taking over the mantle for Daniel Craig’s final three films.

But sometimes, the obvious pick is the right one. Emma Thompson is acting royalty with a commanding air of authority, which is exactly what M calls for. I can just as easily picture her chastising Bond for a reckless bit of espionage as I can see her delivering some characteristically bone-dry British wit. Imagine how fucking electric a Pattinson-Thompson tête-à-tête would be.

Runner-up: Kristin Scott Thomas or Fiona Shaw.

We haven’t had an American Bond Girl since Halle Berry in Die Another Day, a film that, unfortunately, doesn’t hold up on rewatch on account of [gestures at Pierce Brosnan surfing a CGI tsunami]. Let’s have Bond dip back stateside with one of Hollywood’s most exciting young stars—and one whose name already sounds like that of a Bond Girl—in Chase Infiniti. Her resume is small but impressive: the emotional center of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Best Picture-winning One Battle After Another, a supporting role in Apple TV’s Presumed Innocent, and the lead of the Handmaid’s Tale spinoff The Testaments. And if Infiniti’s on-screen work isn’t enough to move the needle, she’s rocked enough red carpet looks to prove she knows how to make an eye-popping entrance. For a Bond Girl, that’s half the battle.

Runner-up: Margaret Qualley, mostly because she basically auditioned to be a Bond Girl at the 97th Academy Awards’ Bond tribute.

Aimee Lou Wood’s vibe as a performer is, in a word, cute. In her most notable performances—The White Lotus and Sex Education chief among them—there’s a natural warmth and mischievousness that would make her a fun scene partner for Pattinson’s Bond. Moneypenny is traditionally the one person at MI6 who can get flirty with Bond without worrying about getting a lecture from M after the fact. Wood has the charm and comic timing to make that dynamic sing.

Runner-up if Moneypenny becomes Irish: Nicola Coughlan.

Pattinson, Anne Hathaway, and (quite deservedly) Samantha Morton have been receiving much of the praise for their work in The Odyssey, but Himesh Patel’s beleaguered Eurylochus might be the film’s unsung hero. Now, he can pivot to playing the Bond franchise’s underappreciated MVP in Q: a perpetually put-upon tech genius who has to watch a reckless womanizer repeatedly destroy million-dollar prototypes. Patel has the dry, exasperated delivery down pat, and he’d be a perfect straight man for Pattinson’s particular brand of chaos (and it would mark a more-than-welcome Tenet reunion). Perhaps Q will belatedly give Patel the accolades he deserved for The Odyssey. (Also known as the Rhea Seehorn Principle.)

Runner-up: Matt Berry in character as Laszlo Cravensworth.

This might be recency bias, because I just watched Kelvin Harrison Jr. in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (say that three times fast). Harrison Jr. is Beetee Latier in the prequel, who was previously played by none other than … Jeffrey Wright. Credit where it’s due: Harrison Jr. does a mean Jeffrey Wright impression in the film.

However, we don’t need to see Harrison Jr. reheat his Wright impression in the new Bond. What I’ve admired in everything I’ve seen him in is how chameleonic he can be—to the extent that you could conceivably cast him in just about any role and he’d find a way to make it his own. (There’s no better evidence that he could play a killer spy than his performance in the psychological thriller Luce, where his character is eerily hard to get a read on.) I want a fresh take on Leiter, and the one thing we can say for Harrison Jr.: he’ll deliver on that promise.

Runner-up: John David Washington for peak Tenet vibes.

Look, I get it: Do we really need Tormund Giantsbane 2.0 in a Bond movie? But Hivju doesn’t deserve to be defined by that role for the rest of his career. He’s got the kind of outsized screen presence that demands an at-bat as a Bond henchman. (You can totally picture him getting excited by Bond drawing blood during a fight.) Sure, Villeneuve isn’t exactly known for humor in his projects, but Bond films have a long tradition of colorful henchmen, and Hivju could dial up the menace without taking himself too seriously. Give him a gimmick, a tweed suit, and no more than four lines of dialogue, and I promise that Hivju will steal every scene he’s in.

Runner-up: Olivier Richters for that Reacher season 3 fight scene alone.

Miles Surrey is a Brooklyn-based culture writer who covers television, film, and whatever your dad is interested in. His work can also be found at The Ringer, Vox, Vice, and The A.V. Club.

#4723. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4722. The 9 Walking Shoes WH Editors Love the Most

These are the pairs we reach for again and again.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

It’s easy to underrate walking as one of the best things we can do for our fitness—after all, it doesn’t get your heart rate up like running or a HIIT workout. But that doesn’t mean you’re not getting tons of physical and mental health benefits from walking, whether you’re following a walking workout plan or not.

And perhaps one of the best things about walking is that it doesn’t require any specialized equipment or gear except a really good pair of comfy walking shoes. Luckily for you, we’re constantly testing walking shoes, and we’ve narrowed down all the options out there to a list of pairs we reach for again and again. We’ve used our testing experience, plus picked the brains of podiatrists and other experts to compile our favorites in this guide.

If you’ve logged even a couple of miles in a not-so-great pair of walking shoes, you know wearing the wrong footwear can make what started out as a nice walk turn into an uncomfortable slog fast (we’re talking blisters, achy arches, plantar fasciitis, and more).

The right walking shoes, on the other hand, can help you walk farther, feel happier while doing it, and gush to friends about your sneakers (ask us how we know). Plus, select styles can help prevent injury or overpronation (when your arches collapse and cause your foot to angle inward), says podiatrist Chanel Perkins, DPM, an assistant professor of foot and ankle podiatry in the Department of Orthopedic Surgery and Rehabilitation at the University of Texas Medical Branch.

After testing dozens of walking shoes for our 2026 Fitness Awards, the Adrenaline GTS 25 took the top spot for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. Our staffers who tested it say it’s comfortable enough to walk in for hours. “It offers just the right amount of cushioning for a bouncy step without compromising on support for my flat, wide feet,” says WH beauty editor Nicole Saunders.

That comfort starts with the 25’s updated midsole, which feels plusher than previous models without losing an ounce of stability. It still features the brand’s signature GuardRails technology—firmer along the sides and softer through the center—to gently lock in your stride. In our testing, Brooks continues to set the standard for stability, making this a standout pick for anyone whose feet tend to roll inward while walking.

When it comes to fit, the 25 has a roomier toe box up front and a secure (but still comfortable) heel lock back, which helps cut down on friction and lowers your chances of blisters during long walks. The higher 10 mm drop creates a slightly forward-leaning stride that takes pressure off the calves and Achilles, making the 25 a smart pick for anyone with tight lower legs or Achilles sensitivity. If you prefer a flatter feel underfoot, though, we recommend something lower profile like the Hoka Mach 6.

At 9.5 ounces, it’s one of the heavier options on this list, but that added weight comes from the stability tech and structured testing. We barely noticed the difference, especially once we got moving.

Diana Rogers, DPM, a podiatric foot and ankle surgery specialist in Crystal Lake, Illinois, and Casey Pidich, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon based in the Bronx, New York, both recommend Hoka’s Clifton series to patients for arch support, so you know it's a good one.

Pidich loves that the design encourages great form—the sole ensures that your feet rock off the ground rather than push off your toes. Rogers specifically recommends the shoe for her plantar fasciitis (a condition where you feel pain in the arch) patients for this exact reason. “The lightweight feel on this shoe propels feet forward rather than making them do extra work,” she says.

WH style editor Shannon Zitz found in her testing that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. “My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe,” she said, noting that her stride felt smooth and natural.

The Clifton 11 is available in wide and extra-wide sizing, making it a good fit for a wide variety of walkers.

Read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro

For those who appreciate a good slip-on shoe, the Skechers Go Walk Flex Azriel’s lightweight, breathable mesh upper is great for sweaty feet, while hovering around a bargain price of about $60 (and on sale for cheaper sometimes). The ultra-cushioned midsole offers great arch support, too.

“This is a solid no-frills walking shoe that’s perfect for errands, quick hot girl strolls, or for walking your dog,” says WH style editor Shannen Zitz. “I love that it slips on easily while still having the appearance of a classic sneaker with bungee laces that never come undone.”

Zitz was skeptical about whether the slip-on would be supportive and secure enough, but the breathable, stretchy mesh offered surprisingly good compression around her feet.

“It keeps my feet locked in and has never caused any pain or blisters,” she says. “While I wouldn’t log miles in this shoe, it is cushioned and supportive enough for long periods of standing or casual wear.” However, she finds the style a bit orthopedic-looking, although the white colorway can look cute with jeans or dresses.

Asics is considered a classic, all-around great brand for walking, especially if you struggle with overpronation (ankles that roll inward) or have flat feet. Take the Gel-Kayano 32, which has thick foam borders on each side to encourage proper alignment and walking gait. Deep heel cups also help keep arches supported—there’s a reason this shoe made our best plantar fasciitis walking shoe guide.

Fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi is a huge fan of the firm, stiffer midsole that still maintains massive plushness with its signature gel cushioning system for superior shock absorption. “My landings feel like I’m hovering above ground, which says a lot given I stomp on hard pavement daily. I actually find it more cushioned than the Hoka Mach 6,” she says. The heel-to-toe drop is 8 millimeters, which Accardi says is a bit high for her liking, but ideal if you want to take all the pressure away from your arches.

The Hoka Mach 7 is Zitz’s personal favorite. While it’s technically a running shoe, she loves it for recovery and walking. “I’ve been living in this sneaker since returning from a week-long hiking trip where I logged about 20K steps per day,” she says. “It’s flexible, lightweight, and cushioned—it basically feels like a hug for my super tired feet.” The cushioning also doesn’t feel bulky compared to other Hoka models, such as the Bondi 8.

The previous iteration, the Mach 6, took home our 2025 Fitness Award for top walking shoe thanks to its blend of responsive cushioning, breathability, and lightweight construction—and the Mach 7 has built on that winning formula with an updated outer and grippier bottom. Zitz tested this shoe after it first dropped, walking more than 150 miles in it—and not once did she feel even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

Another brownie point? It comes in wide sizing. Some WH editors find standard Hoka sizing pretty narrow, but the wide fit has adequate space in the toe box, so you can walk for hours without experiencing any friction. For extra room overall, podiatrist Shital Sharma, DPM, a podiatrist at Pinewood Family Care Co. in New Jersey, recommends going up a half-size in all walking sneakers because your feet tend to swell and expand from physical activity.

Lined with mesh to make this an ultra-breathable sneaker, the Pegasus is a winner because it has a slim, low heel that Perkins says is awesome for maintaining a smooth walking cadence. We love that the 42 is lighter than the previous model and has a curvier toe box that gives more toe spring, a smoother ride, and a roomier fit.

WH Fitness Director Jacqueline Andriakos has worn countless versions of the Nike Pegasus for both running and walking and has logged hundreds of miles in it. “I find the sole a bit on the firmer side, and the mesh upper really hugs and forms to your individual foot shape,” she says. “The shoe feels perfectly snug and secure as you step without being too constricting.”

She does flag that the tongue sometimes gets folded up and tucked under the laces in a slightly uncomfortable way. “I fix this by being really diligent when I put the shoes on, making sure to pull the tongue taut and make sure it's lying flat before tying my shoes.”

The shoe is super breathable and lightweight, which makes it a great option for spring and summer, but less so for cold or wet weather. Overall, this is Andriakos’ go-to walking shoe recommendation for her friends and family—and so far she's only heard happy feedback from loved ones who have purchased a Pegasus shoe.

The latest edition of the Fresh Foam X 1080 wows us with its inclusive sizing, with narrow, standard, wide, and extra-wide fits available to accommodate all feet.

“I have a hard time finding walking shoes that are both cushioned and supportive enough for my high arches and sensitive balls of the feet, but that are also narrow enough,” Andriakos says. “This is absolutely perfect if you deal with any foot pain issues or struggle with sneakers being a bit too wide—I have walked over 100 miles in these at this point and have never even had a sore or tender spot from rubbing or chafing (they also required zero break-in period).”Andriakos also finds the laces are very secure and don’t come untied easily. The only downside? “When I’ve worn it on rainy days, I notice my feet will feel damp and it takes a bit to dry out.” To help combat that, she just throws it in the dryer (which, to be clear, isn’t recommended by the brand, but she found it hasn't damaged the silhouette!).

The On Cloudtilt Remix is built for walking, thanks to its sequence of collapsing “cloud” foam to deliver a smooth, plush ride. It has maximum cushioning and bounce, compared to lots of other walking shoes we’ve tested, making it a solid pick for walkers and casual runners who prefer a softer, cushier feel underfoot.

Zitz recently added this pair to her collection and appreciates how lightweight and springy it feels. “I feel like I have such a pep in my step when I wear it—which is basically all the time since it’s so stylish,” she says. “I love the layers of see-through mesh on the upper, which looks super modern and clean. I’ve been wearing this shoe nonstop with capris, leggings, and athletic shorts.”

This style features Helion Superfoam (a blend of firm and flexible foam components) that delivers bounce without a lot of bulk. It also has a moderate 7 mm heel-to-toe drop, meaning it distributes weight evenly throughout the lower body, making it a pretty good pick for most walkers. It’s the perfect shoe that combines all our must-have walking shoe features into one sleek kick.

The New Balance 608 V5 Trainer has over 38,000 reviews on Amazon, and for good reason. The brand integrated its signature ABZORB midsole (a blend of substantial foam cushioning with compression resistance), which is designed to lessen the blow on joints when walking.

The 608 has tons of shock absorption which makes it great for neutral to high arches. But since it lacks stability features, it’s not our top choice for flat feet. We do like that it comes in narrow, standard, and wide sizing.

Ideally, walking shoes will assist with your gait (your walking pattern) instead of just cushioning impact. Your shoe should also be somewhat stiff—the more it bends, the less stability it will have.

To test the flexibility, hold the shoe at the toe box and heel counter and try to fold the shoe in half by pushing on its ends to see how sturdy it is. If it folds in half or twists with ease, it’s too flexible, says podiatrist Elizabeth Daughtry, MD, a podiatrist and foot and ankle specialist with Foot and Ankle Specialists of the Mid-Atlantic in Cary, North Carolina.

She also adds that seeking out a shoe with a boat-like (rockered) shape, rigid midsole, and firm heel counter can help stabilize feet, control overpronation (collapsing arches), and prevent heel striking.

Look for walking shoes that have an outsole with more rigidity in the midsole for stability. Different feet have different needs, so it’s important to have insoles that can be removed in case you use orthotics. “Most shoes don’t offer adequate support alone,” says Dr. Daughtry. “You should supplement most shoes with a more custom-molded orthotic, which your local podiatrist can make for you, as this provides adequate support and helps with shock absorption, while also allowing for additional cushioning.”

Testing footwear is something we’re a little obsessive about, and we’re testing walking shoes on a constant basis. Over the past year alone, we’ve tested over 100 walking shoes, paying attention to fit, comfort, support, and durability. To narrow it down even further, we also consulted podiatrists and certified trainers about their favorite picks.

Additional reporting by Nicolette Accardi.

#4721. 9 Best Small Sectional Sofas That Are Truly Stylish (2026)

A sprawling living room might be the dream, but having a small space doesn’t preclude you from being able to stretch out on the couch. Sectionals specifically designed for smaller rooms prove that cozy movie nights and afternoon naps aren’t reserved exclusively for those with a massive floor plan. In fact, choosing a sectional with the right proportions stands to make a smaller room feel larger. There’s no reason to settle for a hodgepodge of chairs and ottomans when a thoughtfully selected sectional can transform every seat into the best seat in the house.

Being mindful of a space’s dimensions is always important when shopping for furniture, but especially so with a small room, where every inch may matter. Still, a variety of clever configurations—including L-shaped sectionals designed to nestle into corners, modular designs that are easily rearranged, and sofas with reversible chaises that give you more flexibility—cater to seemingly every layout. Add in performance fabrics, washable slipcovers, and supportive cushions, and you’ve got a recipe for some seriously comfortable yet compact lounging. Ahead, we’re sharing our favorite sectionals for small spaces that ensure every square foot counts.

The best-selling Abisko sectional from Article is made even more beautiful by colorful, performance velvet upholstery. Suitable for those with little ones and pets running around, the fabric is non-absorptive, meaning spills and crumbs won’t stay embedded in its weave. Two orientations—chaise and L-shaped—allow you to Tetris its silhouette into your space as you see fit.

Instead of opting for a giant L-shaped sectional that will take up the entire room, aim for something with a smaller footprint. Available in performance fabric and three leg finishes, this sectional couch is ideal for a tiny living space and a major upgrade from a smaller loveseat thanks to the chaise addition. While not an official fold-out sleeper sofa, the back cushions flop back to give you enough space should you be inclined to nap. Contributor David Kaufman, who tested it out for us, calls it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.”

Similar to the Thuma sectional contributor Evan Russum told us “feels solid and durable,” the Essential Sofa follows the brand’s signature simple-but-considered aesthetic with a minimalist silhouette,rounded cushions, and a grounded wooden base. Raised armrests add sculptural presence without overwhelming a small living room, while the detachable ottoman lets you switch between a left- or right-facing chaise—so everyone can have a turn on their favorite side of the sofa.

Not your average grey couch, AllModern’s Jossa sectional is minimalist in looks but generous on comfort, thanks to its dense foam padding that offers plenty of support without feeling stiff. Easy to de-assemble, the modular design allows the sofa to evolve with your seating needs. Craving two separate lounge chairs? Done. Prefer a love seat? Just slide the two larger seats side-by-side. Today’s layout doesn’t have to be tomorrow’s.

The slim arms and low profile on this this reversible three-piece sectional make the Unwind especially suitable for a limited living area as it doesn’t monopolize the space. Five neutral color variations all come in a linen blend, but olive’s grounding tones are speaking most to us. This sectional, like many of the others on this list, can be configured to be left-facing or right-facing depending on your living room setup, and we particularly like that in case you tend to switch up your design layout (we certainly do).

At just 62 inches wide, Sabai’s Essential Loveseat Sectional demonstrates how even the smallest living rooms can accommodate a proper chaise lounge. The compact design features clean lines, a generously sized chaise, and supportive foam cushions, offering the ideal spot to stretch out after a long day. Adding to the sectional’s appeal is its focus on sustainability. It combines a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)—a third-party verification that ensures ethical wood sourcing—with upholstery fashioned from recycled natural materials. It’s also easy to clean and maintain, largely thanks to its washable slipcovers, sold separately—a welcome feature for anyone whose couch often doubles as a dining chair for meals eaten over the coffee table. Suffice it to say, this sectional is particularly well-suited to apartment living.

CB2’s Deseo sectional brings a little drama to small-space living, courtesy of rich, praline-brown performance velvet, broad arms, and a low-slung silhouette that practically begs you to sink in and stay awhile. The three-piece configuration, matching ottoman, and option for an extra-deep seat only extend the lounging possibilities and allow you to take advantage of every inch of your space. If brown doesn’t fit your space’s palette, worry not; the Deseo comes in plenty of other glamorous colors, including seven other performance velvet upholstery options.

Serious lounging is the goal for Sundays’ Movie Night sectional, with oversized cushions, deep seats, and a relaxed silhouette that makes it difficult to resist the urge to spend the afternoon totally horizontal. The cream linen upholstery adds to its laid-back feel, while the movable ottoman lets you stretch out or create a more open seating arrangement when company comes over. The company’s own LiveLife performance fabric is stain-resistant, moisture-repellent, and washable, with removable slipcovers that make living with a light-colored sofa significantly less intimidating.

Interior Define takes customization very seriously, and the Sloan sectional showcases how having such options can pay off in a small living room. Choose your preferred upholstery, cushion fill, seat depth, and leg style, then fine-tune the dimensions to suit your floor plan. The reversible chaise adds another layer of flexibility, allowing you to change its orientation, in case you rearrange your furniture or move to a new place with a different layout.

Contributor Malia Griggs tested the Sloan in her own 196-square-foot living room, where she found that its supportive cushions, tailored silhouette, and carefully selected dimensions worked beautifully alongside a narrow entryway. “If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space,” she added.

What Features Should I Look for in a Sectional for Small Living Rooms?

Modular furniture—any sectional that comes in several parts so you can adjust your sofa to suit the configurations—is built with flexibility in mind, making it the ideal contender for a small living space. We have tested and loved Castlery modular sofas, but a search for modular sectional should give you plenty of other options. A room tight on space can benefit from couches with storage, like those from Albany Park. Now you’ll be able to minimize the clutter and extra blankets by stowing them underneath your seat.

How Do I Arrange a Sectional in a Small Space?

Don’t fall for the tiniest sectional you can find, but rather invest in something well-made—it plays a big part in your living room, after all. While it may seem counterintuitive, Nashville interior designer Amanda Khouri says, “Filling a small room with small furniture can make it feel…well, smaller.”

Designer Alicia Murphy used a sectional in the living room of a teensy trailer she converted into a plush family getaway in Montauk, New York, for this very reason: “If you use a corner sectional rather than a sofa and chair, you most likely will add seating for two or three more people,” Murphy explains, noting that the alternative prevents you from having about 36 inches of dead space in the corner.”

Another way to make it work? Set an L-shaped sectional across from two club chairs to create a conversation zone, advises interior designer Suzanne Dawson.

What Do I Look for in a High-Quality Sectional?

When you’re working with a small space, quality counts. It’s much harder to get away with a mid-century modern knock-off when it’s one of four furniture pieces packed into the room. When shopping for a sectional, evaluate the materials and care instructions. Avoid anything with plywood, and polyester when you can. Seek out solid wood construction, such as walnut, oak, or teak; and premium fabrics, like linen, leather, or chenille. You’ll also want to keep the warranty and return policy in mind, in case you want to send back a piece that doesn’t work for you.

#4720. 17 New Ways to Jerk Off That Will Make Masturbation So Much Better, According to Sex Experts

If you haven’t changed things up since seventh grade, read this.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

#4719. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

#4718. Before You Plan Thanksgiving Dinner, Plan Family Dynamics

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

By this point in November, many of us have started planning Thanksgiving. We’re discussing who’s coming, who’s bringing what, and whether people prefer the canned or fresh cranberry sauce. We may also be planning conversations that haven’t happened.

Will someone ask about our relationship and whether we’re married yet? Will our parenting become a topic of discussion? Will we spend another holiday doing the work while everyone else watches football?

I have written about the friction that can accompany family gatherings. As Thanksgiving approaches again, I keep wondering would it would look like to prepare for the family dynamics as thoughtfully as we prepare for the meal.

Think about the moment you’re most concerned about. Perhaps it’s a particular question, a familiar disagreement, or the expectation that you’ll organize everything. Now consider what you’re predicting. Are you anticipating a situation that happens regularly? Or are you imagining several possible arguments and preparing a response to each one? Past experiences give us useful information, but mentally replaying an argument doesn’t necessarily give us a useful plan.

Try making the concern specific: “I’m worried someone will comment on my career decision.” Then identify a response you would feel comfortable using: “I’m comfortable with my decision, and I’m not looking for advice about it today.” You may still feel uncomfortable and dread having the conversation but having a response ready simply gives you somewhere to begin.

We often approach holidays with goals that depend on other people, like everyone will get along, no one will make an insensitive comment, or everyone will appreciate the effort. Those hopes are understandable, but they’re also difficult to guarantee.

Consider a few decisions you can make yourself. How long will you stay? Which preparations can you reasonably take on? What will you do if a conversation becomes uncomfortable? You might decide to visit for dessert rather than spend the entire day. You might ask someone else to bring the side dishes. You might arrange transportation so you can leave when you’re ready.

These decisions deserve space alongside the grocery list.

If a familiar pattern bothers you, consider whether there’s a request you can make before the gathering. For example, if you usually manage the meal and cleanup, “I need more help this year” is a starting point. A more specific request gives others a clearer way to participate: “Can you handle the dishes after dinner, including putting the leftovers away?”

The same applies to traditions. If the usual schedule no longer works for your household, raise that issue while plans are being made. Others may be disappointed. You can acknowledge that disappointment while still explaining what you can offer.

In an uncomfortable moment, finding the right words can be difficult. Choose language that sounds like something you would actually say. For an intrusive question: “I don’t have anything I want to share about that.” For unsolicited advice: “I’ll ask if I need suggestions.” For a conversation you want to leave: “I’m going to step away for a few minutes.”

A prepared phrase won’t determine how another person responds. It can help you communicate your own decision more clearly.

Preparation can also include thinking about what you’re looking forward to: Is there someone you’d like to spend time with? A recipe you want to learn? A game, walk, or family story you’d enjoy sharing? Make a little room for that experience rather than assuming it will happen once everything else is finished.

Once you’re home after the gathering, give yourself a fair assessment of the day. One awkward exchange doesn’t have to define the entire gathering. You can appreciate the parts you enjoyed and think honestly about what you’d change next time.

Thanksgiving takes preparation. Along with deciding what belongs on the table, we can decide what we have the time, energy, and willingness to bring to it.

#4716. How to Become Change-Curious

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

We are swimming in a sea of content about change: social media, health and wellness reporting, and advertising (including those little videos at the gas station). Messages about change are inescapable and part of the background noise of everyday life. Often we ignore the onslaught of “be better, do better” messaging, and other times we eagerly try to change ourselves because we so passionately want our lives to be different.

What if we paused for a moment, and instead of forcing ourselves to just do it, we stepped back and shifted toward exploring our relationship with change—to befriend it—so change can increasingly be about wonder and learning and less about stress and avoidance?

Like any troubling relationship, it can be useful to explore some of the dynamics that are not working for us. If we are fortunate to find ourselves changing with ease and little friction, that is a cause to celebrate. For most of us, at least some of the time, we have some difficult experiences engaging in change. We might tell ourselves that change is good; that we should want it. Such a message is difficult to accept when we are not certain change is what we want or need. We might also believe that if we don’t want change, there must be something wrong with us; we are resistant or self-sabotaging or anxious or overwhelmed. Some of these things might be true, but labeling ourselves brings up shame, and shame can be crippling, as it can bring to mind past failures or negative messaging.

Change can also be hard because it takes work. Even if we are completely inspired and motivated to change, developing habits and learning new ways to do things takes time; a recent study found it takes an average of 66 days for a habit to form. For any individual, it can take more or less time for a behavior change to become automatic.

Change is work; it takes time and disrupts our lives. We have cognitive, emotional, and behavioral friction that makes it more difficult to start and complete. Yet, despite the difficulty, we seek change. We want our lives to improve, so we purchase lots of self-help, coaching, therapy, gym memberships, food plans, and surgeries to get started. Across cultures throughout the lifespan, some aspects of change and growth are constantly occurring as we seek to change ourselves and our circumstances.

Given that change is both hard and something we desire, what if we considered approaching the change process with a learner’s mind? Instead of forcing ourselves to endure change or shaming ourselves into it, we can befriend change through cultivating curiosity about all it has to offer. Wondering about change and being open to all the ways we show up in the change process has the potential to make change less daunting.

We have many options to be curious about change.

Noticing change in our environment, and then noticing change in ourselves. We can start by spending some time noticing change in the weather or change in plants. Maybe we notice how construction or demolition is changing a neighborhood, or how our neighbor's families are changing and growing. We can then consider changes in our own experience over the years—in our living situations, job, or social life. We can notice the ones that have been the most meaningful. How did these changes happen? Some changes occur because of luck or circumstances, and it is likely that we were able to take advantage of our good fortune. Some changes occur because we worked hard at making change. How did we do it? What characteristics helped us become a “changer,” and how could we tap into those characteristics if we wanted to change again?

Envisioning what change might look like. This is a common approach to increasing motivation for change. What if we decided we could envision something for ourselves in the same way we read a book or watch a movie? We could envision being in a few different situations and view our story with wonder instead of expectation.

Looking at the process more than the outcome. We tend to be outcome-oriented. We see products that promise to help us build muscle, learn a language, or see younger, more beautiful skin in a few weeks or a couple of months. The promise of relatively quick fixes is so compelling that even when we logically understand there is no way a product can live up to our expectations, we might find ourselves literally buying it. Purchasing a service or product to help us change is not necessarily a problem, and it can be a good thing. Expecting the product to have specific outcomes is where we can become discouraged. So many things impact the actual outcome of our attempts to change: time, environment, our body limits and composition, other demands taking our time.

Shifting our attention to the process requires that we step away from holding the outcome as our top priority. Instead, it’s about going along for the ride and adopting a perspective that we are learning and improving our lives by noticing how we feel after engaging in exercise, making the effort to practice a new instrument, or consuming nutritious foods.

Sampling change. We can check it out and see what it does for us. Events such as Sober October or Dry January were created to help drinkers wanting to explore, but not commit to, changing their drinking behaviors—to test out life without (or with less) alcohol. Virtually any change can be tested out and explored. Sampling a new behavior is not the same as engaging in a dedicated lifestyle change, but it allows for some action. It also provides an opportunity to approach a new way of being in a manner that reduces overwhelm; a chance to wonder about what might be possible.

Curiosity is a powerful frame of mind. It has the potential to tame the intensity of change and open up possibilities for transformation that come from the power of exploration and wonder.

Shigeoka, S. (2024, June 6). How deep curiosity can change the world [Interview by T. Burnett]. John Templeton Foundation. https://www.templeton.org/news/how-deep-curiosity-can-change-the-world

#4715. We've Tested Dozens of Pickleball Paddles. These Are the 10 Best Right Now for Every Type of Player.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Brands like Selkirk and Onix came out on top.

PICKLEBALL GEAR HAS been rapidly evolving year over year, and that just makes the game that much more enjoyable. This sport itself is a great way to stay active, whether you’re looking to crush cardio day, are playing some games for active recovery, or are an avid pickler crushing the competition. The sport itself is still one of the largest and fastest-growing sports in the U.S.—and for good reason—as it has everyone from celebrities, artists, and entertainers to gymgoers (yes, we have a pickleball workout plan) and grandparents hitting the courts. Once you play pickleball, you will quickly realize how important the best pickleball paddles are that suit your style of play—as well as pickleball shoes for proper agility and playing with the right kinds of pickleball balls.

Pickleball paddles have gone through rapid innovation in the past several years due to the sport's rising popularity. We spoke with Ben Johns, a professional pickleball player in the PPA (Professional Pickleball Association) former World #1 and currently top-ranked player on the doubles scene), to get his take on what to look for in a paddle. "The key features you want to look for are weight, dimension, and material," Johns tells Men's Health. Once you know this is a sport for you, here is what he mentions when making that investment buy. "The right time to buy a paddle is usually when you find yourself wanting to improve your skills as a player, as opposed to just playing for fun every now and then."

With the help of Johns (as well as other experts) and a ton of our own testing, we'll outline what to look for when buying a pickleball paddle and detail why these are the best ones we've found.

DOWNLOAD OUR ULTIMATE PICKLEBALL WORKOUT PLAN PDF

When it comes to pickleball, Selkirk leads the way with its fantastic lineup of paddles, and its LUXX Control paddle just may be its most polished yet. At the end of the day, controlling your shot and placing the ball exactly where you want it to go reigns king, and this paddle does that best.

This midweight paddle strikes a balance between high-tech specs and craftsmanship, featuring a slightly longer frame (16.45 inches) and a lengthy handle (5.35 inches), which allows for greater reach and more room to perform a two-handed backhand. The Florek carbon fiber face and thick 20mm honeycomb core provide the accuracy you need without compromising your ability to generate powerful shots.

Having the pleasure of playing with this paddle, I just love the way that it seamlessly cuts through the air. Unlike other cheaper paddles that can create drag, this one does not. It almost feels like my reflexes are quicker when I play with it.

This paddle just does it all, from its modern looks to its accurate shot placements to the power and speed it can create—there's nothing this paddle can't do. With a presence for controlled hits, each shot feels intentional, while still maximizing power. While it may lack the elite pop of others, its overall performance outshines that drawback. With its current reduced price, it's hard to beat, making it our pick for the best overall pickleball paddle.

Head's Radical Elite paddle is the ultimate wallet-friendly pick for those who are getting pickleball fever. As far as design goes, the Radical Elite comes with a honeycomb core, a fiberglass finish, and a wide surface area to smack the ball. You also get a comfortable foam handle with a length similar to that of a tennis racket.

While the Radical Elite lacked power a bit, this paddle prioritizes control while staying lightweight, so it's a great option for learning the game. You can play competitively with the Radical Elite too, but as you see yourself progressing you may want to switch to a paddle with more power. But remember, this paddle retails for around $50, when in reality it plays closer to a $100 paddle. It's such a good price that it makes for an easy pickleball gift you can give to players of all skill levels (experts can use it as a backup paddle).

Made in collaboration with Ben Johns, who has dominated the PPA tour for years, having won an impressive 123 title wins. This paddle is made with enhanced stability, giving you a precise shot from its charged carbon surface. Basically, it’s been bond-treated for improved strength, which gives you a crisp feel during contact for improved energy return on the ball. In a nutshell, this gives you a “poppier” response.

What helps make this one pro-level paddle is the insane propulsion core. It’s designed with a patent-pending core that gives you explosive power unlike any other, on all shots, from line drives, drops, dinks, and counters. Combine that with an elongated paddle face, and you will have ample hitting surface area to make you a spin master with an enormous "sweet spot," meaning fewer miss hits, too. One of the best features is that this paddle is NFC chip-enabled. In a world where data is king, this allows you to access training vids based on your style of play, a community experience, and gamification, all through the JOOLA Connect app. This thing truly is next level.

A $250 pickleball paddle is no easy investment, but those who want premium gear will find the Selkirk Power Air Epic interesting. But it’s no longer regularly priced, and has gotten discounts over the years (it can currently be had between $120 to $187 depending on the website). One of the elite models on the PPA tour, this is one "epic" paddle. For starters, the Power Air has an elongated handle and stand shape that creates a generous surface area, while the handle makes it perfect for double-handed backhands. Second, the Power Air’s performance is some of the most advanced—it’s truly a power player's dream. Selkirk added the air opening to create faster swing speeds, as it feels like serves have some extra whip to them.

A third key finding from playing with the Power Air Epic was the overall feel of the paddle. It's like holding the paddle equivalent of a Ferrari: fast, lightweight, sexy. The handle is luxe and cushioned, and the extra wrapping near the end of the handle helps you get a more secure grip. There are no pronounced edges on the Power Air for the ball to take a weird shot off of, so there's actually a chance you get a clean return even if you connect near the edges of the paddle.

The Power Air Epic is meant for serious players only (and the price tag reflects that), and the sleek design shows that you're using the best technology in the game.

If you watch any professional pickleball events on TV, it's likely you'll notice Onix as a paddle in a few pro's hands. Onix has a wide array of paddles to choose from, but the Graphite Z5 is a trusted pick that's big on ball control and clean returns. The takeaway from the Z5 is that you get the best qualities of a graphite paddle for a price point of just under $100, which is an excellent value. Graphite is a favorite for many pros due to the material's strong design and lightweight feel, making it easy to control each shot and finesse where you want your ball to go.

It plays with a well-balanced feeling in the hand. The Nomex honeycomb core seems to limit dead spots, and the paddle offers enough space to connect cleanly on most shots. (The shape of the paddle gives you a sneaky amount of surface area, too.) In terms of quality, the paddle has a lofty weight and powerful sweet spot, giving it a superior rating. The paddle was especially great on serves, allowing you to whip the ball over the net and get some good spin. The Z5 caters to all skill levels, but it's especially great as a beginner pickleball paddle—you won't have to upgrade from it for quite a while.

Once you've played the game long enough and can consider yourself an advanced player, you need a paddle that demands more than just control. You need a paddle that can deliver heavy line drives, insane spin, and provide all the pop and power you can imagine. That is exactly what you get in the SLK Era Power paddle.

Its fusion core is a blend of polypropylene honeycomb surrounded by EVA foam, increasing its overall stability and taking its forgiveness to another level—something you don't find too often in a power paddle. I love that even when I miss the sweet spot on a hit, it still feels stable in my hand, which means I can worry less about having to make perfect contact each time. A rare thing for elongated paddles.

Its elongated shape, measuring 16.5 inches with a 5.8-inch handle, provides great reach on every shot and ample space for double-backhands. Combined with its three-layer face of fiberglass and T700 raw carbon fiber, shots on this paddle seem to jump off its surface (according to Selkirk's website, this paddle can generate speeds up to 2,000 rpm). This paddle is excellent for aggressive players.

While its price may be a bit of an investment, and there is a bit of a learning curve with elongated paddles like this, its overall performance easily outweighs those setbacks, especially for advanced players. If you're seeking a pro-level paddle that swings well, puts ample pop on each shot, and looks good doing it, the SLK Era Power is for you.

For those looking to put their shots on "spin cycle," the Quartz paddle from Six Zero is for you. The face of the paddle is crafted from raw textured T300 carbon which gives it the perfect hitting surface for maximum traction on the ball. Translation: more rpm and way more spin. Then, you also have the lightweight design, allowing for way faster swings and quick hands, which again can translate to more revolutions on the ball. Not only does it give you top-tier spin, but it has a great flexibility to give you good control over your shot placements, too.

It has a solidly large sweet spot for shot forgiveness, and thanks to its one-piece unibody construction, it was also designed with durability in mind. For a paddle that is performance-driven and for a price under $100, this is one of the best paddles on our list. They also have multiple pops of color that wrap around the head of the paddle and really stand out on the blacked-out face, so there’s a choice for everyone, too.

If you want a nice and wide paddle for maximal surface area, the Project Boomstik in the widebody model is the way to go. So, why would you want a wider paddle if it means a slower swing speed? Well for starters, widebodies are great for forgiveness and minimizing mishits. The Project Boomstik gives you a generous sweet spot and is a perfect choice for those who love to work the net in the kitchen (where the game is truly won and lost).

With this Selkirk model, you get a nice and long handle too, which makes it an even greater choice for defensive players who prioritize paddle and ball control. And even though most would consider this a defensive player’s choice, it’s loaded with Selkirk’s BoomCore tech to help give it plenty of pop on all your power shots. Plus, it makes for one heck of a durable paddle.

While it is arguably one of the most expensive off-the-rack models you can buy, if you wanna dominate the competition, even as a rookie, this one will get the job done.

The one paddle that I have been [patiently] waiting to get my hands on is this highly anticipated Honeyfoam TKO-X model, which builds on the brand’s super successful Reserve special edition model. At the heart of its build is the proprietary three-foam design that gives it even more energy return delivering excellent power on every shot. The ball jumps off the surface, so much so that it took a couple of points for me to adjust (but in a good way). Once I got it figured out, my opponent was left scrambling to return my aggressive forehands. Its advanced edge guard also dampens shock quite well, no matter how much power I put into it.

But, it’s not all power no touch either, as I could easily control shots in the kitchen as well, making it a surprisingly well-rounded paddle. This is partially thanks to its elongated design, which makes those hard-to-reach shots just that much easier. While it is one of the most expensive options in our guide, its soft touch and great power make this my new favorite competitive paddle.

If you’re looking for a paddle to make a statement on the courts and one that can easily fit in at a country club, Modest Vintage Player is that paddle. Its pro heritage model aesthetic is one inspired by the brand’s exceptional work with leather. It’s also perfectly complemented with a carbon fiber head, which ensures this pick is more than just a pretty paddle, as it performs quite well, too.

With a generous sweet spot and slightly oversized face, this paddle is a great choice for players of all levels, which helps you maintain optimal control. It weighs 8.6 ounces, which means you also get plenty of power on shots when you whip around on your strokes. The 4K weave carbon fiber surface gives it a nice responsive pop while the paddle's thickness perfectly balances accuracy and power. The slick blacked-out face perfectly matches the chestnut brown leather grip. Plus, with its air scoop design, you get the feel of a pro-level paddle for half the cost, yet this one gives you all the heritage vibes you could want.

The average weight for a paddle is going to be around 8 ounces and fluctuates above and below that number. Anything at 9 ounces is usually too heavy and anything under 7 ounces is usually too light. "For weight, somewhere in between 7.5 to 8.3 ounces is a good range," says Johns.

The basic configuration most new players will want to use is called a "wide body paddle" according to Carl Schmits, Managing Director of Equipment Standards & Facilities Development for the USA Pickleball Association. "This configuration is easiest to maneuver and is also good for a controlled, more defensive style of play. Paddles that are close to 8 inches wide by 16 inches long are within the wide body category," says Schmits. "Players that have well-developed stroke mechanics from other sports may be most comfortable with paddles having a longer shape (between 16" and a maximum of 17") and some with a longer handle will better facilitate two-handed backhands, which is an increasingly common grip used very successfully by tennis converts."

Carbon fiber and fiberglass composites are the two most common materials used in high-quality paddles, as they have been shown to help players deliver speed and spin on the ball. A good pickleball paddle should also have zero dead spots, meaning when you make a quality hit on the ball it doesn't randomly underperform and fall flat. "When it comes to the material, I like to look for a polypropylene core with a fiberglass or carbon fiber face," says Johns.

Similar to how you might shop for a driver in golf, your pickleball paddle is going to have a formula of power and control that works for you. A power paddle will have a tight sweet spot and deliver a shot with more pop, while a control paddle has a larger sweet spot that's softer but allows for more consistent returns.

For a power paddle, look for something tighter and more compact in all areas of the design."Paddles that have thinner cores, like a 13mm-14mm, have longer configuration, and typically made with fiberglass faces will return more power, although hitting the ball with heat is as much a result of an efficient kinetic chain as anything," says Schmits.

If you want a paddle with more control, a design with maneuverable dimensions and a carbon fiber face (as opposed to a fiberglass face, which is harder) is recommended. "I'd look for at least 8 inches of width on the paddle head and for a thicker core that's 16 millimeters or more, or 5/8 inches or more," says Johns.

Our experts explained to us grip circumference carries just as much importance in a pickleball paddle as it does in a tennis racket. They also noted there are fewer options when it comes to shopping for specific grip sizes for pickleball (most brands use a standard 4.25" size). Most pickleball paddle grips will vary from just under 4" and no bigger than 5.5".

John Crowley Sr., the Sr. Category Merchandising Manager of Paddles at Pickleball Central, recommends starting with a smaller grip first (when picking between two paddles) and then adding an overgrip if needed. "Very few manufacturers offer different grip sizes and materials, so customizing with an overgrip wrap is the best way to build up the grip to a comfortable size," added Schmits.

A reliable pickleball paddle is usually thick, as brands fill the interior space with their own technology to limit the odds of any dead spots. One popular interior makeup is a polypropylene core (also called honeycomb core design) which is a type of interior webbing that's made into a honeycomb shape to ensure the paddle is evenly balanced.

I have been fortunate enough to play with numerous paddles over the past couple of years, from multi-hundred-dollar paddles to those under $50, and I can tell you that it’s not always about the cost that makes a paddle worth playing with. Through my time playing regularly and testing gear along the way, I've combined that experience along with paddle recommendations from the Men's Health editors and writers who also play consistently. For this guide, we considered everything when we compiled our list of recommendations, including weight, dimension, material, grip circumference, core design, aesthetics, feel, and price. Once I gathered all our notes, I compared paddles based on performance and durability. We also considered what paddles appeal best to specific skill levels, from beginners to 4.0-rated players.

After testing tons of different pickleball paddles and consulting with experts, we eventually landed on 10 pickleball paddles we recommend for 2026.

Just like shopping for running shoes, you can find pickleball paddles at all types of prices. Generally speaking, expect to pay anywhere from $60 to $100 for a beginner- to intermediate-level paddle. If you're looking for an advanced paddle, any model we recommend above $100 is a worthy choice.

If you're going to play more than two times a month, Johns says it's time to invest in a paddle: "The right time to upgrade your paddle is usually when you find yourself wanting to improve your skills as a player as opposed to just playing for fun every now and then."

Crowley Sr. also gave us tips on how to go about investing in a paddle. "When you go shopping have a budget in mind (the best value to price is no object). How much do you plan to play? What is your sports background and if you know, what style of player are you—power player, control player, or all court?" he says.

If you think you have to splurge on a competition-ready paddle, think again. "I say shoot for the $75 to $100 range for your first paddle if you want to play competitively," says Laura Gainor, USA Pickleball's Director of Media Relations. "And if you’re planning to sign up for your first tournament, make sure your paddle is USA Pickleball approved." We agree there's nothing worse than bringing your paddle to a match and discovering you need to find a different one that complies with the rules.

Fiberglass and graphite paddles have characteristics about them that can play to your natural strengths on the court. "You are trying to find the recipe that works best for you," says Crowley Sr.

In general, fiberglass pickleball paddles have more power but less control than a graphite paddle. This is mainly due to the fact fiberglass weighs more. Graphite, on the other hand, is lighter and stronger due to the thinly layered construction of the material. Graphite paddles are often associated with better control, resulting in a better ability to place each return where you want it.

Fiberglass paddles are more wallet-friendly, and have been gaining in popularity due to their quality performance while staying at a good price point. Graphite paddles are more expensive and are often seen being used more by pros in tournaments.

One other paddle material to consider is composite. For example, you might find a composite design that incorporates carbon fiber and fiberglass in hopes of bringing equal parts control and power. Composite paddles are usually high quality and exist at graphite-level prices (or higher), but it's important to make sure the paddle is USA Pickleball approved if you ever want to play competitively.

While all of the paddles above were curated with attention to sweet spot, there are a few characteristics you can prioritize when shopping.

The first is to go by surface area. You will probably get the most sizable sweet spot area by going off the most common dimension of a 16" length and 8" width paddle. Second is inner material of the paddle: look for a trusted core material, like a honeycomb propylene core design, that can cover all areas of the paddle and help reduce the chance of there being any dead spots.

Last is the type of material used to construct the paddle. There are a lot of fiberglass paddles out there with generous sweet spots, but if you want to get the largest sweet spot possible then going to a more expensive graphite paddle is probably the best move.

There are two situations where you want to consider replacing your paddle. The first is if you find yourself playing more (and perhaps more competitively) than when you first started. A good rule of thumb is if you're playing more than two times a month, it's probably time to consider investing in a competitive play paddle.

The second situation that would warrant replacing your paddle is if it's damaged or worn down from constant play. If you stick to the paddles we recommend above, you can expect the lifespan to last between 1 to 3 years. But sometimes your paddle can wear out faster (also called a "dead paddle") if you're playing much more. In order to tell if you need to replace your paddle due to overuse, pay attention to the feel and how the ball comes off the paddle. Is it returning or serving shots the same way it was in the first few months of use? If not, your paddle is probably wearing down.

You can also pay attention to the sound of the ball off the paddle. Are your best shots delivering a nice and clear pop? Or are they sounding flat and droopy? If you're out playing consistently, then you will probably know when your paddle is ready for retirement.

Pickleball paddles are resilient. They can take a beating on the court, but off the court you should keep them away from the sun and heat for extended periods of time.

If you're concerned about keeping your paddle pristine-looking, invest in a paddle cleanse kit to clean the face, and pack it in a paddle cover to prevent scuffs. "I wipe down my paddle face once a week with water to prevent any accumulation of dirt," says Schmits.

"Keep your paddle stored in a cool, dry environment and never leave it in a hot car. Also, don't smash it when you're angry," says Johns.

Like any sport, pickleball does pose some injury risks (some games can last over 2 hours at a time). The most common injuries include tennis and golf elbow, which can be caused by swinging a paddle that's too light or too heavy—or simply by swinging it too much and not allowing for proper rest.

"Grip size, paddle weight, and swing weight (how the weight is distributed) all contribute to the efficiency and comfort of the human-paddle interface," says Schmits. "A grip that is too small may require an over-clenched grip to prevent spinning in the hand, a paddle that is too light may not have enough mass to prevent twisting on off-center shots and will transmit unwanted vibration, an overly head-heavy paddle may require more torque to snap through. Also, a paddle that is too heavy will quickly fatigue muscles, as well as slow down hand speed."

A paddle with good vibration absorption is also important, which is why a wooden paddle is a no-go if you're an active player. "Anything that absorbs more energy in the paddle and reduces the amount of vibration that travels up your arm is good at preventing soreness," says Crowley Sr.

Jeff Turbett is a fitness and wellness writer who's based in Miami, FL. His work has been featured in The Manual and FightCamp.
