#4714. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4712. After a Year of Washes, These Towels Are as Plush and Absorbent as the Day I Got Them

Utah-based bedding, bath, and loungewear brand Cozy Earth has built a $100 million business around bamboo. The brand is perhaps most loved for its luxe sheets, but we’ve also tested (and generally loved) its pajamas, blankets, and cotton-and-bamboo towels. In fact, most of our shopping team owns at least one Cozy Earth product, regarding them as “ultrasoft pieces that will reign forever in our linen closets,” as senior shopping editor Nashia Baker puts it.

The brand’s bamboo sheets have taken best overall in both our bamboo and cooling sheets roundups. Its towels have earned their own spots in our guides on the most absorbent bath towels, the best quick-dry towels, and the best waffle towel sets. Contributor Megan Wahn was sold on the waffle bath sheets after dunking a corner in a bowl of water: “I could literally see as the parts of the towel that were not submerged soaked up the water,” she says.

Towel marketing tends to promise softness and absorbency in the same breath, but in my experience, it’s rare that both are true. Cozy Earth’s Luxe Bath Towels are the exception. After a full calendar year of countless showers, followed by washing in New York City laundromats, where the dryers have one setting (and it’s “inferno”) they are still exceptional towels.

The feel was memorable from the start: plush and not the least bit scratchy. At 600 grams per square meter (GSM), a unit of measure for a towel’s weight, it also has real heft. The towel’s blend of cotton and bamboo viscose, woven using what the brand calls zero-twist technology, leaves no fabric loops for your hand to catch on. But despite lacking the shag-carpet texture of some fluffy towels, this soft, smooth Cozy Earth model remains absorbent enough to dry you with ease.

A year later the most impressive quality of these towels is how little they’ve changed. They’ve been through more showers than I can count and a year of intense washes (the care label calls for tumble drying on low, an option my laundromat doesn’t offer), and they’re still as soft to the touch as when I first got them. Plenty of cotton towels demonstrate their best absorbency in their first months, and then never again. The Cozy Earth Luxe towels still dry me off as well as they did on day one, which is something I can’t say for most towels I’ve owned (and I’ve tested a lot of them). In my experience, plush towels go stiff and absorbent ones go thin, but these have done neither.

The one concession to the laundromat is color. My off-white pair of towels has picked up a faint blue-gray tint over the year, though they still pass for white. For this I blame the machines more than the towels, which deserve better care than I can give them….

At $118 (currently $88.50 for Black Friday), I won’t pretend the Luxe Bath Towels set isn’t an investment. You can buy a 12-pack for the same price on Amazon. But these are my favorite bath towels due to their durability as much as their feel—a luxe combination that’s hard to replicate on a tight budget. Towels that stay soft and absorbent for a month are easy to find; it’s much rarer for options to hold their quality for a year and beyond. If you’re replacing a full bath-towel set, I recommend starting here instead of cycling through cheaper towels that end up costing you the same once you’ve replaced them a few times.

To outfit the whole bathroom, Cozy Earth sells the Complete Luxe Bath Bundle. The hand towels and washcloths are just as good as the towels.

#4711. Self-Affirmation, Self-Integrity, and You

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Brief self-affirmation activities have been reliably shown to help people change and grow by reducing a perceived threat. But what kind of threat do they reduce? And how does self-affirmation reduce it?

The vulnerability to stereotype threat we discussed in Part 1 of this series is grounded in a basic human need to see ourselves as “adaptively and morally adequate”: good, capable, reasonable and sensible people who are able to achieve the outcomes that matter to us.1 Named the self-integrity motive by Claude Steele, the psychologist who identified it,2 it differs from the better-known construct of self-esteem in that it is our motivation to view ourselves as “good enough,” rather than to maximize our positive thoughts and feelings about ourselves.

Our sense of self-integrity can be based on any valued qualities we believe we possess.3,4,5 Unfortunately, our self-integrity can also be threatened by anything we see as reflecting negatively on who we are: failure, bad things that happen to us, criticism or rejection, information that challenges what we believe, recognition that we’ve acted in ways that conflict with our values—any experience we take as evidence that we are bad, wrong, incompetent, irrational, foolish, or unable to deal effectively with life.

We feel bad about ourselves (ashamed, humiliated, unworthy) when our self-integrity is threatened, which triggers defensive efforts to protect or restore it: We may dismiss or minimize the threat; attack its source; marshal evidence against it; rationalize or justify our behavior, or deny being responsible for it; try to puff ourselves up through self-aggrandizing statements or comparing ourselves with people who we believe are worse.6,7,8 Any of these strategies may reestablish our self-integrity, but only temporarily—and they leave us vulnerable to more of the same kinds of threats.

This is where self-affirmation can change the story. Focusing on important or valued aspects of the self that are not affected by the self-integrity threat bolsters our global sense of being “good enough”— protectively, if we self-affirm before we feel threatened, or restoratively, if we self-affirm afterward. It also makes all our defensive responses unnecessary, and in doing so promotes honest self-awareness and constructive responses to the challenges we face. Put simply, self-affirmation creates a protective buffer by putting the threat in perspective and helping us take a broader view of ourselves: Yes, I may have been wrong, made a bad decision, acted in a way I regret—but I’m a good and capable person, and my flaws and mistakes don’t define me.2,4,9

The research on self-affirmation shows how it benefits us in concrete ways. Self-affirmation increases our acceptance of information about risks to our health that would otherwise feel threatening.10,11,12 It increases our openness to evidence that challenges dearly held beliefs, and decreases our tendency to evaluate arguments for and against those beliefs in favor of what we already believe.13,14 It reduces the mental energy spent ruminating on failures and flaws and frees our mental resources for more productive activities, improving performance under stress on tasks that require focused attention, problem-solving, creativity, and insight.9,15,16,17 It increases our self-compassion and fosters helping behavior toward others.18

Most broadly, self-affirmation activities have consistently been shown to enhance the well-being of those who engage in them:9 It improves the general sense of feeling good, of having community and belonging; it offers relief from symptoms like depression and anxiety that create barriers to well-being; and it improves one's sense that they are a person of competence and value. And just as in the case of the studies of women dissatisfied with their weight that we began with in Part 1, these effects on well-being are long-lasting and get larger with the passage of time.

Can self-affirmation make a difference for you? Here’s an activity that will allow you to experience it for yourself. (For the most meaningful experience, please have paper and pen ready. And please do each of these steps in turn, waiting until you’ve finished the one you’re doing to go on to the next, rather than reading ahead to the end.)

1. Think of an area of your life that you have been struggling with. It could be a behavior you’ve been trying to change, but have not changed; something you’ve been wanting to do, but have not done; a decision you’ve been trying to make, but have not made. Once you identify it, please spend the next minute just thinking about the struggle and what it has been like for you.

2. From the following list, please choose one value that a) is very important to you, and has been important in your life, b) is not related to the area of your life you have been struggling with.

3. Think of a time when the value you chose was important to you. For the next few minutes, please write about that time and why that value was important to you.

Self-affirmation is most powerful when we’re facing a challenge of high personal importance, which is when our self-integrity is most likely to be threatened.19 Because self-affirmation works by focusing us on an aspect of ourselves that we feel good about and that does not feel threatened, it’s important to choose a value that’s unrelated to the challenge at hand; trying to affirm a threatened aspect of the self often makes us more defensive rather than less.19 And self-integrity is strengthened the most when we affirm “self-transcendent” values (values that express concern for others), rather than values that primarily benefit ourselves.4

The positive effects of self-affirmation on how we feel and how we act reinforce a key tenet of motivational interviewing: we’re most likely to change and grow not when we feel sufficiently bad about ourselves, but when we feel accepted and valued.20 When you embark on a path toward change, don’t neglect to focus on what makes you worthy of value and respect just as you are.

2. Steele, C.M. (1988). The psychology of self-affirmation: Sustaining the integrity of the self. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 21, 261-302.

3. Steele, C. M., & Spencer, S.J. (1992). The primacy of self-integrity. Psychological Inquiry , 3, 345-346.

4. Cohen, G.L. & Sherman, D.K. (2014). The psychology of change: Self-affirmation and social psychological intervention. Annual Review of Psychology, 65, 333-371.

5. Aronson, J., Cohen, G., & Nail, P.R. (2019). Self-affirmation theory: An update and appraisal. In E. Harmon-Jones (Ed.), Cognitive dissonance: Reexamining a pivotal theory in psychology (pp. 159-174). American Psychological Association.

6. Buckingham, J.T., Lam, T.A., Andrade, F.C., Boring, B.L. & Emery, D. (2019). Reducing contingent self-worth: A defensive response to self-threats. The Journal of Social Psychology, 159, 284-298.

7. Spencer, S.J., Josephs, R.A., & Steele, C.M. (1993). Low self-esteem: The uphill struggle for self-integrity. In R.F. Baumeister (Ed.), Self-esteem: The puzzle of low self-regard (pp. 21-36). Plenum Press.

10. Epton, T., Harris, P.R., Kane, R., van Koningsbruggen, G.M., & Sheeran, P. (2015). The impact of self-affirmation on health-behavior change: A meta-analysis. Health Psychology, 34, 187-196.

#4710. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4709. The Best Electrolyte Powders, Tested by Registered Dietitians

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our team recommends formulas from Thorne, Transparent Labs, and LMNT.

ELECTROLYTE POWDERS HAVE become very trendy over the last few years, but the variety of ingredients and numerous products on the market may leave you wondering what you actually need. These powders have various amounts of sodium and other electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium, etc.), plus sugars and additional ingredients meant to improve your hydration after a sweaty workout. Based on our extensive testing, we found that these formulas are an easy and convenient way to replenish electrolytes lost in sweat. That's because sweat contains water and electrolytes, with sodium losses being the highest, says Leah Reitmayer, MS, RD, a Board-Certified Sports Dietitian and owner of Lettuce Eat Dessert.

The American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) recommends a sodium intake of 300 to 600 milligrams per hour for endurance athletes who exercise for over two hours or are considered “heavy sweaters,” losing more than 1.2 liters per hour. Important: The average person doesn’t need an electrolyte supplement after your average one-hour workout. But when you need that extra boost of hydration and electrolyte replenishment, we have the seven best electrolyte powders to choose from, according to sports dietitians and athletes.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, it’s my job to find the latest and greatest equipment and supplements, including electrolyte powders. I personally tested each of these products in a variety of scenarios, including as part of a morning routine, in the afternoon after work, and after intense workouts, in the gym and on the track.

I also consulted Marty Munson, Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach; and Deputy Editor Paul Kita to get their insights on the electrolyte products they have tested throughout their years in the industry. Read on for our guide to the best electrolyte powders.

*Additional reporting by Kelsey Kunik, RDN.

I’m a big fan of Thorne because they design their supplements so that they can be used by the most elite athletes but are also accessible to everyone else. This formula provides a balanced blend of sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium. And in keeping with their no-BS approach, there aren’t any sweeteners, colors, or fillers, keeping the blend non-GMO and gluten-free.

Poured into the glass, the powder dissolves quickly and completely, leaving only the color and refreshing taste. I’m a fan of the flavors, which they kept to three heavy-hitters, and if you’re not picky, I recommend the variety pack so you can switch between them.

We’ve seen that brands have been smartly moving away from carbohydrate formulas, so that you can customize your carb intake if you’re an athlete. That is the case here, with only a single gram of carbs. So if you’re looking for a quality, easy-to-drink electrolyte powder that can also travel with you, this is the best.

Transparent Labs Hydrate electrolyte powder includes multiple electrolytes and other nutrients like taurine and Senactiv, an adaptogen complex that supports muscle recovery. “It has 500 mg of sodium per serving, which fits ACSM’s recommendation for sodium replacement per hour,” says registered dietitian Sarah Alsing, MS, RD. You’ll also replace small amounts of potassium, magnesium, and calcium.

Each dose has 1,000 milligrams of taurine, a sulfur-containing amino acid that may help support muscle recovery. You can choose from six flavors, all sweetened with stevia, as this formula is carbohydrate and calorie-free.

“I look for supplements to be third-party tested so you can trust the ingredients listed, and Transparent Labs is third-party tested,” says Alsing. It’s Informed Sport Certified, meaning it’s been tested for substances banned by major athletic regulating organizations, which gives peace of mind to competing athletes.

This electrolyte powder only comes in a multi-serving tub, which could be seen as a downside if you want to take your electrolytes on the road often. But for us, it is a great way to reduce waste and if you’re taking electrolytes as part of your daily routine, you’re probably usually taking them at home.

Experts and testers we consulted with say LMNT is a serious electrolyte supplement, providing 1,000 milligrams of sodium in each pack. With this much salt, you can expect the flavor to be, well, salty. After a 10-mile run or a hard, sweaty bike ride, we appreciate the replenishment, but the salty flavor may take a little getting used to for some people. However, other athletes like Munson actually prefer that taste over some typical sports drinks, which can taste overly sweet. Personally, I tend to agree. The instructions include mixing a packet with 16 to 32 ounces of water, but you can always dilute it a little more to cut the salty flavor. I drink mine with about 12 ounces of water, and find the salty taste to be a bit stronger but still enjoyable at these proportions.

“There are several flavors to choose from, which helps finding one you will enjoy and tolerate during your workouts,” says Alsing. You can choose from fruit flavors like citrus or watermelon or even a more decadent chocolate caramel. It’s sweetened with stevia leaf, and one packet has just 2 grams of carbohydrates. If you don’t like the taste of stevia, you can always choose the raw, unflavored option with no sweeteners added. Personally, I stick to the fruity flavors as I feel the salty taste is best when combined with citrus, berry, or melon notes.

In addition to sodium, LMNT provides 200 milligrams of potassium and 60 milligrams of magnesium, electrolytes that are also lost through sweat, although in lower amounts than sodium. Personally, I find that drinking these electrolytes right in the morning keeps me better hydrated throughout the day.

Not only is Nuun Sport Powder certified gluten-free, but this product is also vegan and kosher. The Nuun tablets are effervescent, which can be difficult to drink while running or biking. But the Sport Electrolyte Tablets have no fizz, making it a better option for athletes drinking them on the go. The powder sticks come in five flavors and have just one gram of added sugars along with stevia for a sweet flavor. While many people love the packet flavors, they are a lot stronger than the tablets, which may be off-putting for some athletes if you’re drinking them during a workout.

Each packet has 300 milligrams of sodium, along with potassium and magnesium, making it a good all-around hydration drink for workouts lasting an hour or less. The packets are easy to tear and mix quickly into a water bottle for hydration on the go—no waiting for tablets to dissolve. And while Nuun is known more for their tablets, we find the powder packets to be the superior form when it comes to mid-workout hydration.

This formula has 330 milligrams of sodium in each serving and is free from gluten, soy, and certified vegan. This formula does have 7 grams of added sugars and a total of 9 grams of carbohydrates but is also one of the few that does not use stevia as a sweetener. Though 7 grams of sugar is higher than zero-sugar brands, it’s a lot less than some competitors use (for example, Liquid I.V. has 11 grams of added sugar per serving).

And unlike the other powders, this one has 15 percent DV of zinc, an essential trace mineral that helps with the absorption of water and electrolytes by the intestines, aiding hydration.If you’re looking for a zero sugar option, they have the Zero Sugar Variety which also has the addition of several B vitamins.

Liquid I.V. has been in the electrolyte game a while, but their original product contains 11 grams of added sugar. To keep up with competitors boasting formulas sans sugar, they released a sugar-free line and it does not disappoint. This updated formula is one of our favorite sugar-free electrolyte powders on the market, sweetened instead with stevia and allulose (a naturally occurring, low-calorie sugar that doesn’t spike blood glucose).

Each stick delivers 500 milligrams of sodium, which meets ACSM’s recommendations and is ideal for heavy sweaters or endurance athletes. You’ll also get 370 milligrams of potassium, but you won’t find any magnesium or calcium in this product—which could be a miss for those looking for a complete electrolyte supplement rather than the heavily sodium-focused product here.

It’s worth noting that Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free does contain vitamin C, niacin, and B vitamins, added micronutrients that many electrolyte supplements do not offer. This formula mixes easily into water and comes in unique flavors like white peach and rainbow sherbet. Just be aware that the sweetening agent allulose, while generally well-tolerated, may cause mild bloating or gas in some people.

First and foremost, not everyone needs an electrolyte powder (or an electrolyte drink) every day. In fact, the average American is getting way too much sodium in their diet, contributing to chronic health conditions like heart disease and high blood pressure. “The average man working out for an hour a day can meet their electrolyte needs through what they eat and should prioritize drinking plenty of water,” says Alsing. She recommends eating potassium-rich foods like bananas, avocados, and potatoes, and salty foods like salted nuts or pickles after a sweaty workout.

If you’re unsure whether you would benefit from an electrolyte powder, talk with a registered dietitian, or try a product like the Nix Hydration Biosensor, which measures your sweat output in real time. Marty Munson—Health Director at Men’s Health, triathlete, and USA Triathlon Certified Coach—says sweat testing played a big role in helping her customize a rehydration plan. For those who have done the research, talked to their doctors, and are sweating more than most recreational athletes, we’ve got the scoop (pun intended) on what to look for in the best electrolyte supplements below.

“You want to look for a product that contains at least 230-690mg of sodium,” says Reitmayer. This is in line with the ACSM recommendations to replace sodium losses after two hours of exercise or exercise that results in heavy sweating. Losing just 1 to 2 percent of your body weight through sweat can lead to an increased heart rate, higher core temperature, as well as decreased cardiac output, time to exhaustion, and power. Sodium helps maintain fluid retention in the body, leading to less water loss and improved hydration status as you drink water to replace what you lost through sweat.

Electrolyte powders vary widely in sugar content. We recommend looking for options with no more than 5 to 10 grams of added sugar unless you’re using it as both a hydration and carbohydrate source during longer workouts. For casual training or daily hydration, sugar-free options using stevia, monk fruit, or allulose are usually preferred. Be mindful of sugar alcohols, which can cause bloating or GI discomfort in some people.

If you want to combine your carbohydrate refueling and electrolytes in one drink, look for a formula that has a carbohydrate source. Munson explains that the trend is going away from these types of drinks, as many athletes like to have more control over their refueling source, choosing a separate powder for electrolytes and using other mixes, gels, or chews as an energy source. Some electrolyte powders have no carbohydrates, while others may contain 15 grams or more. “If you are looking for a sports drink with electrolytes, aim for 5-10% of the solution carbohydrates,” says Reitmayer.

Sodium isn’t the only electrolyte lost through sweat, even though it is the most abundant. You may also want an electrolyte powder that replaces electrolytes like potassium, magnesium, chloride, and/or zinc. While it’s helpful to replace these electrolytes as well, some athletes prefer less magnesium, as forms of this mineral can have a slight laxative effect, which you would probably want to avoid while competing.

How you plan to use your electrolyte powder should factor into the packaging you choose. Single-serving sticks or packets are great for travel, races, or throwing in your gym bag. They’re lightweight, easy to portion, and reduce mess when you’re on the move. Multi-serving tubs can be more cost-effective and environmentally friendly, but they require measuring and aren’t as convenient mid-workout or on the trail. Either way, look for resealable, moisture-resistant packaging to keep the powder fresh and free from clumping.

Electrolyte powders can be used before, during, and after exercise to help replace fluids lost during periods of long exercise or heavy sweating.

Replacing water and sodium helps to avoid the effects of dehydration, which could include an increase in heart rate, core temperature, and muscle glycogen use and a decrease in cardiac output, cognitive awareness, anaerobic power, and time to exhaustion. All of these can have negative effects on performance.

Any exercise where you’re sweating can lead to electrolyte losses. Short sweat sessions can usually be replaced with the sodium included in regular foods and drinks, while sessions longer than two hours may need a stronger source of sodium, like an electrolyte rehydration drink.

Depending on the ingredients, some electrolyte powders could lead to digestive upset, especially if they include high amounts of sugar, sugar alcohol, or magnesium. Drinking electrolyte powders when you’re not losing sodium through sweat or if you have high blood pressure could increase your blood pressure.

#4707. What Else Is True?: Lessons About Suffering and Healing

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Twenty years ago, I helped establish a nonprofit organization called the Trauma Resource Institute. I could not have imagined where that decision would take me, the people I would meet, or how profoundly the journey would change my understanding of human suffering and resilience. My work has brought me into communities experiencing extraordinary adversity. I have witnessed the aftermath of natural disasters, the heartbreak of war and conflict, and the suffering of people whose lives have been disrupted by trauma, violence, and loss.

Yet, amid the suffering and the heartache, I have encountered something else. I have witnessed extraordinary courage, generosity, humor, creativity, kindness, and compassion. I have seen people reach toward one another as their own lives unraveled. I learned that suffering can profoundly alter the course of our lives, but suffering is never the only truth about who we are or what remains possible.

Throughout my work, I have returned again and again to a simple question:“What else is true?” When something terrible happens, what else is true? When we feel overwhelmed by loneliness, grief, or fear, what else is true? When the world seems divided or hopeless, what else is true? This question is not an invitation to deny suffering nor does it ask us to turn away from injustice, grief, trauma, or pain. Rather, it invites us to widen the lens through which we experience ourselves and the world.

Alongside fear, there may also be courage. Alongside grief, there may be love. Alongside helplessness, there may be one small place where choice still exists. And sometimes, amid tremendous suffering, hope begins to emerge. We can grieve and still experience gratitude. We can feel frightened and still recognize moments when we feel safer. The presence of suffering does not erase our capacity for well-being.

One of the most profound discoveries is that trauma is not only a cognitive or emotional experience. It is also physiological. Our nervous systems continually respond to what is happening around and within us. When we perceive danger, our bodies mobilize to protect us. Our hearts may race, our muscles tighten, or we may become numb or disconnected. These responses are not signs of weakness but reflect our biology working to help us survive. The body carries a wisdom that words alone cannot always express. Our nervous systems communicate distress and danger, but they can also register safety, connection, comfort, strength, and possibility.

The Trauma Resiliency Model (TRM) and Community Resiliency Model (CRM), approaches I developed, make knowledge about trauma and the nervous system accessible. Central to these models is body literacy: learning to recognize and understand the sensations through which our bodies communicate. People can begin to tell the difference between sensations of distress and well-being without judgment. Distress does not necessarily disappear, but it need not be the only experience available to us.

As my understanding of trauma deepened, I began asking another question: What if knowledge about our nervous systems did not remain only within therapy rooms? This question flooded my waking moments: What if teachers, nurses, parents, children, first responders, and entire communities could learn simple skills to restore well-being?

These questions changed the direction of my life. I have watched people adapt CRM and TRM wellness skills for schools, hospitals, shelters, recovery programs, disaster response, and communities affected by war and other disasters. I have learned that resilience grows between us. Our nervous systems respond to the presence of others. A caring voice, a compassionate expression, or the steady presence of someone we trust may help us feel safer and more connected.

I invite you to consider your own life's journey: Who or what has lifted you when you stumbled? Who or what reminded you of your worth when you doubted yourself? When loneliness or despair entered your life, who or what helped you reconnect with hope?

As I reflect on this journey, I find myself increasingly drawn to the idea of human flourishing. Healing from trauma can open possibilities beyond the reduction of distress. As people experience greater safety and physiological regulation, there may be more room for curiosity, creativity, meaningful relationships, purpose, and joy.

Flourishing does not mean living without pain, nor is it an inevitable outcome of adversity. It is the possibility of living with greater meaning, connection, and agency while acknowledging life's complexities. Communities flourish when compassion becomes action, human dignity is protected, and people recognize their shared humanity.

I no longer think of hope simply as optimism about the future. I understand it as an openness to possibility, even when we cannot predict what comes next. Hope may begin with an unexpected kindness, a moment of physiological steadiness, or discovering that we still have a choice. After twenty years, I continue returning to the question that has accompanied my journey: “What else is true?”

Sometimes the answer is someone I love. Sometimes it is the generosity of a stranger, the beauty of nature, or the quiet recognition that my body can still experience peace in the midst of chaos. And sometimes the answer is simply that I do not yet know what else is possible.

Resilience reminds us that suffering never gets to tell the whole story. Within the human spirit, the wisdom of the body, and the connections we share, another truth may be waiting to be discovered—a possibility for connection, healing, and hope.

I began this journey wanting to help people recover from trauma. Twenty years later, the people I have met have taught me something equally important: Even in a world filled with suffering, our capacity for compassion, connection, and hope remains one of the most remarkable expressions of our shared humanity, and it provides a pathway to healing. And fundamentally, the body has a wisdom that words cannot speak.

Miller-Karas, Elaine (2023). Building Resilience to Trauma: The Trauma and Community Resiliency Model, Second Edition. Routledge.

#4705. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4704. Experts Warn That a Deadly Disease That Causes ‘Immune Amnesia’ Is Surging in the U.S.

This week, the United States officially lost its measles elimination status, after 26 years. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which oversees measles elimination status, said in a statement on Tuesday that the U.S., along with Bolivia and Mexico, “lost their status after the same measles virus lineage circulated uninterrupted for 12 months or more.”

But measles cases have surged in the U.S. throughout 2026. The most recent CDC surveillance stats on measles report 5,412 confirmed cases in the country, with 47 states affected. Given that measles hasn’t been a large problem in America for decades, it’s fair to be unsure what to think right now.

Doctors fall squarely into the “very concerned” camp for a few reasons. “Measles is not a trivial infection,” says William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine.

Not only can measles be miserable to experience, but it can also cause lingering effects that can lead to everything from deafness to brain infections, Dr. Schaffner points out. Measles can even cause something known as “immune amnesia,” where your body’s immunity to a range of pathogens is basically wiped out. (More on that in a moment.)

Here’s what infectious disease doctors say:

Meet the experts: Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York; William Schaffner, MD, an infectious disease specialist and professor at the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine; and Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

Measles, which is also known as rubeola, is a very contagious viral infection, per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Measles is so contagious, in fact, that up to 90 percent of people who come into contact with someone with the virus will get it if they’re not protected (like through the vaccine).

Measles usually causes symptoms like a cough, runny nose, tiny spots inside the mouth, a rash, and a high fever. It can also lead to severe complications like pneumonia, immune amnesia, and encephalitis (aka swelling of the brain). “Even with uncomplicated measles, people are usually miserable for a week,” Dr. Schaffner says.

Measles can also cause “immune amnesia,” meaning the virus can wipe out memory B cells and memory T cells that your immune system has built up from previous infections. “There’s a window after having measles where your immune system has taken a hit, and you have increased susceptibility to viruses, pneumonia, and diarrheal illness—it’s a real thing,” says Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York. This can last for several months, or possibly even longer, he says.

Again, measles was considered eliminated from the U.S. back in 2000, meaning the virus wasn’t considered to be spreading in the U.S. While the country did see some measles cases, they were usually in people who had visited other countries. However, according to the latest CDC stats, only 18 of the 5,412 confirmed cases were from international travelers this year.

Cases began slowly creeping up last year, with CDC data showing 2,289 cases were reported. This trend continued when, this July, a little over the halfway point of the year, there were already 2,318 cases reported. At the time, Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, noted that this was the highest number of cases seen since the disease was considered eliminated from the country. “Cases were higher only in the early 1990s.”

Doctors agree that lack of vaccination is the big element behind this increase in cases. “It’s all about vaccination,” Dr. Russo says. “The anti-vaxx movement is more potent now, and they’re winning.”

With fewer parents giving their children the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine, measles cases are creeping back up, Dr. Russo points out.

#4703. 4 Types of Dead-End Relationships

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Sara and Keith have been married for nine years and have three children. Both work full-time, do their share of chores and parenting, and fill weekends and many evenings with soccer games, ballet lessons, or overflow work. Is it an okay life? Yes, they would agree it is okay, but in the next breath, they'll admit there’s little affection or intimacy between them.

I’ve met hundreds of couples like Sara and Keith whose relationship has been pushed to the back burner, and intimacy has essentially reached a dead end.

Here are four of the most common relationship patterns:

Child- or work-centered. This is Sara and Keith. Essentially, they stopped being a couple and instead became mom and pop or worker bees. Such couples often complain that they wish they had more time for couple time, but they're so busy with work and kids.

Roommates. If they don’t have the demands or distractions of work or children, many couples downshift to roommate status. They do spend time together, which they usually enjoy; they may even describe the other as their best friend, but the affection has long since dried up. And like roommates, there’s plenty of talk about schedules and chores.

Parallel lives. This takes the roommate scenario to another level. No best-friend status; no doing things together; each does their own thing; they essentially just share the same space.

Habit/routine-driven lifestyle. This can bleed into all the above variations, where, like Sara and Keith, they do what they do because they do it. They run on autopilot most of the time, and habits and routines kill any hope of spontaneity or anything different.

What holds all these types of couples together is that they're defined by bad solutions to other problems lying beneath. Here are some of the common sources:

Problems that are swept under the rug. If problems go unresolved, they stack up and act like a wedge pushing you apart. You create a long list of "things we don't talk about" and fill in the space with the demands and distractions of work and kids—or you devolve into parallel lives.

A power struggle. Here, problems are never solved because the individuals are unwilling to reach win-win compromises. Sometimes this attitude is fueled by anger and resentment from old wounds; sometimes it is simply a matter of personality—perhaps high anxiety they try to manage through control, self-centeredness, or a need for power. Neither is willing to bend because it feels like letting the other guy win, and coming out on top is always the priority.

Conflict avoidance. Some individuals have learned to fear conflict and others' strong emotions, often because of a childhood environment in which parents were frightening or modeled passivity and avoidance. As a result, anger is internalized or turned into self-blame, and problems are never discussed or resolved. Periodically, one person may act out or explode in anger, which only further fuels their fear and internalization.

Unhealed wounds. Past affairs and sudden, traumatic decisions, such as abruptly quitting jobs or being forced to move—painful incidents that shattered safety and trust and linger, coloring the relationship—have become a grudge that is always there; an open wound that never heals.

An expired relationship contract. Whatever Sara and Keith needed from each other nine years ago, they likely no longer need it now. Each has grown into different needs and desires, but like many couples, they’ve built a life in a box of rules and routines that no longer fit them. Some couples divorce; others, like them, downshift their relationship.

If you’re ready for a change—to get your relationship back on the front burner and bring back intimacy and affection—here are some tips to get you started:

Acknowledge the state of the relationship. In some ways, this can be the hardest step. Like "The Emperor's New Clothes," it requires breaking the code of silence, refusing to ignore reality, and having the courage to be honest. Once you say how you’ve been feeling and start that conversation, you can’t unsay it or the other can’t unhear it. You’ve opened the door to change, and that’s a good place to start.

Change the emotional climate through action. Resist the urge to think change is about getting the other person to change: this leads to nagging, manipulation, or a blink contest where each waits for the other. Instead, think about changing the overall emotional climate of the relationship, breaking ingrained habits and patterns, and stopping autopilot behaviors. The key is action: Plan a date night; snuggle together on the couch while you watch a movie; move the kid’s bedtime earlier so you have time as a couple to simply chat at the end of the day. Something, anything that is different and positive.

Repair old wounds. I’ve heard partners say they just need answers to questions that have been lingering for years—about the affair, the job, or the move. Or sometimes it is just the opportunity to get things off their chests and finally feel heard and understood, without avoidance or defensiveness. Sometimes you can do this on your own; sometimes it helps to start by writing a letter or email; sometimes you need to bring in a professional to help mediate and moderate the conversation.

Tackle unresolved problems. The best way to do this is to chip away at them in baby steps. I suggest that couples set aside a good time to talk when they’re not tired or distracted. Treat it like a staff meeting at work: Set an agenda with one or two items, focus on you, and work toward a win-win compromise while controlling your emotions. Meet for 30-45 minutes. And if it is hard to do, bring in a professional.

Resist the urge to think your feelings need to change before you can act; if you keep doing what you’re doing, you’ll keep feeling the same way. Instead, challenge yourself to break out and take action.

Taibbi, R. (2019). Doing couple therapy. New York: Guilford.

#4702. How You Can Use an Upper-Lower Workout Split for More Gains

If you want to build strength and muscle, split your workout plan in two.

THE STRUCTURE OF your workout over the course of weeks and months should depend on more than just the latest fitness fad. When you’re working toward a goal—whether that’s tied to building muscle, forging strength, losing weight, or improving performance—you’ll have the most success if you follow a plan. That plan (often called a workout split) should take into account arange of factors, including your specific goals, your experience level, schedule, and available equipment.

And one of the most well-known (and easy-to-understand) approaches to this is the Upper-Lower split, which is one of several workout splits organized around training different parts of the body on different days.

An Upper-Lower Split program is broken down exactly as its name implies. One day you’ll train the muscle groups in your upper body (think chest, shoulders, back, arms); then the next you’ll train your lower body muscles (quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves). In general, that means your upper body gets to recover on days you’re training your lower body, and vice versa.

This approach is one of a handful of training splits that works very well if you’re trying to add muscle, or if you’re somebody who’s chasing body recomposition. If you’re trying to build muscle, the more frequently you can train a muscle group with effective, hard sets, the better.

And an upper-lower split lets you train each muscle group at least twice a week, with solid rest in between each session. You’re training each muscle group more frequently than you would if you were doing a bro split (training just one body part a day). And you’re able to do more sets and exercises for key muscle groups than you would if you were doing a full-body training split.

Let’s break down the details of the upper-lower of split, along with a sample session you can use to put it into practice.

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 steps per leg

Sets and reps: 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg

IF YOU WANT to understand the logic behind the workout above, here’s what you need to know. You'll alternate focusing on the upper body muscles and the lower body muscles in this split. Since you're no longer training the entire body, you'll have the time and energy to include a few more accessory motions. Over the course of the week, aim to hit all of the following movement patterns.

There are multiple ways to build an upper-lower split depending on your goals. But in general, think about including three to five exercises in every session.

YOU’RE ABLE TO hit major muscle groups more completely by splitting the body in half. Since we're able to add in a few accessory motions, we can start training in several different planes of motion, too. This split is well suited for recovery, since your upper body rests while you're working the lower body, and vice versa. That allows you to increase your frequency of training.

YOU’RE STILL WORKING quite a few major muscle groups in a single workout, which can be fatiguing for the accessory movements added onto the end. If you’re in the awkward schedule space between having three and four days you can train, you might struggle to hit the upper/lower/upper/lower cadence that will be most effective—so stick to the more flexible full-body split.

#4700. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4699. BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

The enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

There’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a big deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 users reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

For example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

But you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

That’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

When shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

The 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

The Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

The Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

For someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

The Apex 200 launches November 4, with the standalone unit starting at $1,099 during the November 4–18 super early-bird promotion.

Founded in 2013, BLUETTI allows millions of users across more than 120 countries to stay safe and prepared. Its in-house R&D supports a range of solar generators and home backup systems for outage preparation, RV travel, and off-grid living and recreation.

Shop the Apex 200 and launch bundles, and use ELECTREK5OFF at checkout for an extra 5% savings.
