#4697. Anorexia and the Gut-Brain Connection

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

For generations, scientists and doctors believed the brain was the unquestioned command center of the body. It sent instructions and the rest of the body obeyed. Today, we know the relationship is far more complicated.

Your digestive tract is home to an intricate network of more than 100 million nerve cells—so many, in fact, that scientists often refer to it as the body's second brain. Known as the enteric nervous system, this remarkable network coordinates digestion, communicates with the immune system, influences hormone production, and remains in constant contact with the brain inside your skull.

These two "brains" are linked by an elaborate communication system known as the gut-brain axis. Messages travel in both directions, carried by nerves, hormones, immune cells, and chemical messengers produced by the trillions of bacteria that live within the intestines. It's a constant conversation—one that helps regulate not only digestion, but also mood, stress, appetite, memory, and behavior.

This discovery has transformed the way we think about both physical and mental health.

For decades, psychiatrists understandably focused almost exclusively on the brain. Depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, ADHD, and anorexia nervosa were viewed as disorders of brain chemistry. But over the past 20 years, an explosion of research has revealed that the gut is an active participant in all of these conditions. Rather than functioning as separate organs, the gut and the brain operate as partners. When one suffers, the other often does, too.

That insight is especially important in anorexia nervosa.

For people with anorexia nervosa, this two-way conversation has profound implications. Recovery isn’t only about restoring body weight or correcting abnormalities in the brain. It’s also about rebuilding a healthy digestive system capable of supporting the brain’s healing processes.

One of the cruelest aspects of anorexia nervosa is that the illness often convinces people that food and eating are problems.

As recovery begins and eating increases, many patients experience bloating, constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, and a feeling of fullness after only a few bites. These symptoms can be frightening. They seem to confirm the eating disorder's central lie: See? Eating makes you feel worse.

But that's not what's happening. In most cases, these digestive symptoms are not caused by eating. They are caused by starvation.

When the body is deprived of adequate nourishment for weeks, months, or years, it begins conserving energy wherever it can. Digestion slows dramatically. The muscles that normally move food through the stomach and intestines become less active. The stomach empties more slowly, intestinal motility decreases, and constipation becomes common. Food remains in the digestive tract longer than it should, producing bloating, abdominal discomfort, and an uncomfortable sense of fullness after meals.

Ironically, the very symptoms that make eating difficult are often the result of not eating enough in the first place.

Understanding this dynamic can be enormously reassuring as it shows that the digestive system has not been permanently damaged. The symptoms are signs of a body adapting to prolonged starvation and so, as nutritional rehabilitation progresses and the gut begins receiving the nourishment it needs, digestive function usually improves—although it often takes weeks or months for the gastrointestinal tract to recover fully.

In anorexia, another important change occurs deep within the intestines, where trillions of bacteria collectively known as the gut microbiome reside. These microorganisms help digest food, produce vitamins, regulate immune function, maintain the integrity of the intestinal lining, and manufacture compounds that influence the brain. Like every other living organism in the body, they depend on a steady supply of nutrients to thrive.

When food intake becomes severely restricted, then, the microbiome changes as well.

Over the past decade, researchers have consistently found that people with anorexia nervosa have a gut microbiome that differs significantly from those of healthy individuals. Some beneficial bacterial species decline, while others become more abundant. Overall microbial diversity—the hallmark of a healthy ecosystem—often decreases. These changes are now believed to contribute not only to digestive symptoms, but also to inflammation, anxiety, and difficulties with weight restoration.

The good news is that the gut is remarkably resilient. Unlike many organs, the digestive tract is constantly renewing itself. Cells lining the intestines are replaced every few days. The microbiome is continually adapting to changes in diet, medications, stress, and environment. Even after prolonged starvation, the digestive system has an extraordinary capacity for recovery—provided it receives the nourishment and support it needs.

Eating enough food. No supplement can substitute for dietary rehabilitation. Restoring adequate calories, protein, healthy fats, and food-delivered vitamins and minerals remains the cornerstone of recovery from anorexia nervosa.

Digestive enzymes. Digestive discomfort can make every meal feel like a battle. Bloating, cramping, constipation, and abdominal pain often reinforce the fear that eating is making things worse. Breaking that cycle sometimes requires giving the digestive system additional support while it heals. One of the simplest ways to do that is through digestive enzyme supplementation.

Digestive enzymes help break food into smaller molecules that can be more easily absorbed by the body. Although digestive enzyme supplements have not yet been studied in anorexia, decades of clinical experience suggest they can can substantially reduce gastrointestinal discomfort during nutritional rehabilitation.

Probiotics. Another important tool is the use of probiotics—live, beneficial microorganisms that help restore a healthier balance within the gut microbiome. For centuries, traditional cultures have consumed probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, kimchi, miso, and sauerkraut. Today, probiotic supplements provide carefully selected bacteria strains that can help replenish beneficial microbes disrupted by illness, antibiotics, stress, and prolonged food restrictions. Their companion nutrients, known as prebiotics, serve as food for these beneficial bacteria, helping them grow and flourish.

Learn more in my new book, Finally Nourished: A Science-Based Plan to Correct Malnutrition in Anorexia Nervosa—and Achieve True and Lasting Recovery.

Kleiman SC, et al. The Intestinal Microbiota in Acute Anorexia Nervosa and During Renourishment: Relationship to Depression, Anxiety, and Eating Disorder Psychopathology. Psychosomatic Medicine. 2015 Nov-Dec;77(9):969-81. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4643361/

Fan Y, et al. The gut microbiota contributes to the pathogenesis of anorexia nervosa in humans and mice. Nature Microbiology. 2023 May;8(5):787-802. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10159860/

#4696. This Football Manager Lost 90 Pounds in 6 Months Thanks to This Swimming and Walking Routine

The 64-year-old swapped the dugout for the pool and says he feels better than he has in years.

Scottish football manager Steve Evans is “feeling the best I've felt in years and years” after 90 pounds in just six months. After Rotherham dropped him in March last year, Evans decided to focus on improving his health before jumping straight back in at another club.

And it's worked wonders for the 64-year-old, who has meticulously stuck to the plan prescribed to him by health specialists and trainers. It hasn't been easy for Evans, but he's managed to improve his diet and increase his activity levels to a point where he now swims 2.5km every morning, cycles regularly and gets in plenty of steps by walking his dogs daily.

“Here we are six months or so later, six and a half stone down,” he told Sky Sports. “It has been incredibly hard work, but I am feeling the benefit now mentally and physically, feeling fantastic.”

After waking up and taking his dogs on a walk first thing in the morning, Evans then grabs his swimming trunks and heads to the pool at his local gym. While there, he'll swim at least 2.5km, though sometimes further if he's feeling good in the water. Evans also cycles on the exercise bike at the gym to supplement his training, as well as spending some time sitting in the sauna.

In total, Evans spends around two-and-a-half hours in the gym, while he ensures he keeps his diet healthy with lots of protein and a reduced calorie intake. And, if he still has some energy left at the end of the day, the 64-year-old will take his dogs out on another walk in the evening to add a few more steps to his daily total.

Evans couldn't just jump straight into that level of activity, however. He needed to take gradual steps to build up to the 2.5km he now swims everyday, after recognizing that he had started to neglect his health while working as a football manager.

“I came out of Rotherham and within a few days made some family decisions,” he told Sky Sports. “I sat down with the family and, despite the phone ringing from a couple of clubs, I made the decision to get healthy and fitter. It's something I hadn't done for a lot of years. I went to see some serious people and some specialists, a cardiologist and fitness people. We came up with a plan and my family did not think I would be able to do it.”

“I was worried about myself,” he admitted. “My doctor at Royal Papworth gave me a plan. That plan was obviously a substantially reduced intake of calories and a gradual fitness program to then go and work with a fitness coach.”

“It started off with swimming 10 lengths of a pool, which I found really tough at the time, and doing so many walks and so many jogs, to building up to now where I comfortably go and swim 70 to 80 lengths every morning. I had to make sure that I was mentally in tune with that—it's been brilliant and I'm feeling the best I've felt in years and years.”

Having worked so hard to achieve such impressive results, Evans isn't intent on stopping any time soon. Indeed, he's targeting even more weight loss and will look to add some strength and conditioning work in the near future to further contribute to his lifestyle change.

“It's a little bit more weight loss for another two-to-three weeks, and then hopefully by that time it'll be about conditioning, which will be another tough part to go through, but I'm looking forward to the challenge,” he added. “My body internally is actually in really good shape now after all the scans I had last week.”

Ryan is a Senior Writer at Men’s Health UK with a passion for storytelling, health and fitness. #4695. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

#4693. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4692. AI Is Going to Make Us Work Less

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

AI is going to make us work less. All of us.

Most of our grandparents worked six days a week. Nobody called them workaholics; that was simply what a job was, until society decided that Saturday belongs to people. I believe we are approaching a decision of that size again.

I don’t know whether AI will create as many jobs as it destroys or whether most professions will collapse. That is the argument most people are having, and it is worth a minute of context before I get to what I actually want to say.

The optimists say this is like every previous revolution: Some jobs will disappear, new ones will emerge, and people will use AI to become more productive. The World Economic Forum says so, for example (1). The pessimists say this time is different. Machines are beginning to perform intellectual work once reserved for highly educated people. The International Monetary Fund says so, for example (2).

When our professional skills lose their value, what is threatened is not just our income but our sense of relevance: the feeling that we have value in the world, contribute something important, and make a positive impact on others.

But there is another layer that I believe will unfold quite quickly: AI will not only change how we make a living but how much of our lives we are expected to spend doing this work.

I will say it plainly: this is an optimistic post. I intend to earn the optimism with numbers.

Look at the past 130 years. The human condition of work has gradually improved. The workday became shorter. The six-day workweek became five. Paid leave, retirement, sick days, and limits on child labor became part of the social contract. Today, a growing number of organizations are even experimenting with four-day workweeks (3, 4).

None of this happened because work suddenly became less important. These changes were fought for through collective bargaining, legislation, and political struggle. But rising productivity made them economically possible. Society gradually decided that human life should not be consumed entirely by labor.

If an employee can complete in two hours what previously required eight, there are only a few possible outcomes: The company can demand four times as much output. It can fire most of the team. Or society can begin converting some of the productivity gain into time.

The first two options may dominate at first but they are difficult to sustain as a final equilibrium.

An economy cannot function well when a small group labors while millions of capable people have no work, and no sense that they contribute. Workers are also consumers, parents, taxpayers, and citizens. Wages are not only a cost companies pay; they are the money customers spend, and no one can keep selling to people who no longer earn. A system that converts greater productivity mainly into human exclusion would eventually undermine both economic demand and social stability.

The figure below shows what this means in numbers. As dollars stop arriving in ordinary paychecks for common households, whether because jobs disappear or because pay shrinks, what businesses can sell falls with them. By the time roughly 12 dollars out of every 100 have moved, the drop is already the size of the Great Recession. (If you want to see exactly how I built the figure, the note below it is where I geek out.)

This all brings us to thia conclusion: The more stable direction is not a world without work but one in which work occupies less of everyone’s life.

We can already see the cultural preparation for this shift.

People of my generation, those who entered the workforce around the turn of the millennium, were taught to admire sacrifice. In high-tech, working 50 or 60 hours a week was almost a badge of honor. The company was a family. If you left at 5:00, perhaps you were not serious enough.

Many younger workers no longer believe this story. Research on Generation Z consistently finds greater emphasis on balance, well-being, and meaningful work than on climbing the corporate ladder (7).

They want to close the laptop at 5:00 because they have a life. This is often described as laziness, entitlement, or fragility. I think Generation Z may simply be early adopters of a better social norm.

Work can be meaningful. It can make us feel useful, needed, and relevant. But it is not the whole of human existence. We mostly feel relevant by raising children, helping friends, creating, learning, loving, being present, and taking part in communities.

From this perspective, the real promise of AI is that it may finally make the 35- to 40-hour workweek look as outdated as the six-day workweek looks today.

The same way it happened last time. Ford moved its factories to a five-day week in 1926, but not out of generosity: Henry Ford had concluded that people who work all the time have no time to buy anything, and that his workers were also his customers. The weekend was built partly on the arithmetic of the figure above, and the rest by the unions that demanded it and the laws that made it the default.

All three of those engines are already turning. Trials across six countries have shown that companies can drop a workday without dropping output. In Iceland, such trials ended with unions negotiating shorter hours, or the right to them, for roughly 86 percent of the country’s working population (8). In the United States, autoworkers’ union put the 32-hour week on the bargaining table in 2023. It did not win, but the first people who demanded a weekend did not win either. Ford himself said in 1926, “The eight-hour day was not the ultimate, and neither is the five-day week” (9).

Here is that century drawn as what it really is: a staircase that stopped, and a next step already penciled in. The note underneath is where I show my homework.

The transition may be brutal. We will need new taxation, new labor arrangements, and probably several failed experiments. But the direction seems clear.

A few days ago an hawk stopped in the middle of my street. I had somewhere to be. I stayed for a minute anyway.

That minute produced nothing. It was the best one of my day.

The most human outcome of the AI revolution may be a world in which people have more time to be human.

1. World Economic Forum (2025). Future of Jobs Report 2025.

2. Georgieva, K. (2024). AI Will Transform the Global Economy. Let’s Make Sure It Benefits Humanity. International Monetary Fund.

3. Messenger, J. C. (2018). Working Time and the Future of Work. International Labour Organization.

4. Fan, W., Schor, J. B., Kelly, O., & Gu, G. (2025). Work time reduction via a 4-day workweek finds improvements in workers’ well-being. Nature Human Behaviour, 9, 2153–2168.

5. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (2024). Consumer Expenditure Survey, 2023. Quintile figures as compiled by Hernández Kent, A., & Rodgers, W. M. (2025), That Extra Money: A Primer on Discretionary Income, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

6. Petev, I., Pistaferri, L., & Saporta-Eksten, I. (2011). Consumption and the Great Recession. In The Great Recession. Russell Sage Foundation.

7. Deloitte Global (2025). 2025 Gen Z and Millennial Survey.

8. Haraldsson, G. D., & Kellam, J. (2021). Going Public: Iceland’s Journey to a Shorter Working Week. Autonomy and Alda.

9. Ford, H. (1926). Why I Favor Five Days’ Work With Six Days’ Pay. Interview with S. Crowther, World’s Work.

10. Whaples, R. Hours of Work in U.S. History. EH.Net Encyclopedia of Economic and Business History.

11. Huberman, M., & Minns, C. (2007). The times they are not changin’: Days and hours of work in Old and New Worlds, 1870–2000. Explorations in Economic History, 44, 538–567.

12. Eurofound. Records of the French statutory 35-hour week (in force 2000) and the 35-hour week in western German metalworking (introduced 1995). European Foundation for the Improvement of Living and Working Conditions.

13. Eurostat (2025). Actual and Usual Hours of Work. European Commission.

#4689. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4688. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

#4687. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

#4685. The 11 Best Backpacks for Men Who Commute, Lift, Travel, and Do It All

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Top options from Fjällräven, Bellroy, Yeti, and more.

A BACKPACK IS one of your closest gear companions, no matter whether you’re adventuring on asphalt or dirt. We grew up throwing these things over our shoulders as we towed books and lunches to school and beyond. But now you’re an adult and you deserve a backpack built for your present-day life.

In short, a top-shelf backpack can do way more than just schlep. It can wear with such ease that you barely even know it’s on your person, whether you're hiking 10 miles or strolling to the subway stop. It can organize and protect valuables, insulate, and even fend off bad weather and thieves alike. And it can wow with sophisticated features like magnetic clasps and special storage areas tailor-made for very specific devices.

As with running shoes or smartwatches, there are a lot of subcategories within the category itself. There are hiking backpacks built for the trail and brief stays out in the middle of nowhere. There are hydration packs engineered for outdoor pursuits like running and more. And there are travel backpacks made for frequent fliers.

Here, we're after high-use backpacks with everyday appeal. You know, the kind that gravitate as much to the morning bike commuter as to the person headed to the coffee shop with their laptop or even away for the night, not wanting to leave any essentials behind.

There are some nice little details at play with this, our favorite everyday backpack for everyday activities. The angled rear zipper adds some character, as does the well-placed fox logo of the well-known Swedish brand. The pack wears comfortably and the fleece-lined top pocket is ideal for things like mobile devices or sunglasses.

This one is right at home in class, at the gym, on the bus, or thrown in the back of the car while embarking on a weekend adventure. The material is surprisingly rugged and can stand up to everyday wear and tear.

While we're not exactly sure what makes this backpack windproof, we did appreciate how fast it dried after getting doused (not to mention its water-resistant makeup).

Our runaway in the most comfortable department, the Borealis from The North Face had the most organic fit. We've been wearing this bag for quite a while, and the brand's sturdy reputation and our own experiences really solidify this one.

The design really makes wearing the pack effortless, no matter how full you fill it. We loved that it can easily handle a laptop of up to 16-inch screen size and the lumbar support was so ample that even after full days out and about, there was never really a reason to take the thing off. When you do end up taking it off, the standup design makes it super easy to load and the iconic bungee straps just plain look nice (and double as nice means of attaching extra gear). The tech pocket is helpful and lined for extra protection and the sternum strap provides even more stability while on the move.

Watch out for certain colors subject to significant discounts. You might end up with a super deal if you don't care as much about that sort of thing. On campus, on the trail, or at work, this is a great all-around backpack.

We love this pack because it feels both classic and modern at the same time. There's a timelessness to the pack, affording you some extra style points to go along with all that rear cargo space. While it doesn't look it, the pack can easily accommodate a laptop of up to 16 inches. Of the many backpacks we tried, this one had one of the most ergonomic builds, tracing the contours of the back surprisingly well for such a classic model.

We also love the little touches like the small leather insignia and the fact that the zippers stay tucked under the main seam so as not to catch and accidentally open. It also doesn't hurt that it's mostly made from recycled polyester and comes with a significant six-year warranty.

There's a breeziness to wearing this one while out and about and it makes hauling essentials feel more like a task you look forward to.

We fell for this backpack the moment we threw it over our shoulders. That's because it gracefully walks that tightrope between two major pillars in functionality and style. The modern aesthetic not only makes for a cool look but a streamlined design that will have you feeling all the more aerodynamic, no matter what you're up to.

Bonus points to July for the five-year warranty and fabric with a little more heft that can even stand up to some inclement weather. Touting one of the best liners for inclement weather, this backpack is ideal for the biker. Even when you're cycling to work in the rain, this pack will keep things dry and organized. Speaking of the latter, you can do some serious compartmentalizing inside as it's chock-full of thoughtful dividers, pouches, and sections.

Wear it more casually or buckle the chest strap for a more secure fit as you pedal hard up a steep incline. Admittedly, the bag is quite attractive and it's so nice not to have to worry about precipitation of any kind as you go about your business. We did notice that when lugging around a full water bottle or two, the volume was somewhat impeded, but we found workarounds (like a proper water bottle holder on your bike frame) and thought the bag overall functioned at a very high level.

After a triumphant Kickstarter campaign, the latest morphing backpack from Peak Design is here. We sang the praises of this brand at the top of the story and we're going to do the same again here. Quite simply, the outfit understands the hybrid bag concept. Turns out, you don't have to have a 2-in-1 bag that, well, looks and wears like a 2-in-1 bag.

This one is as slick as they come, with intelligent features and an aesthetic that comes off more like a single contemporary bag. The bigger base can do 30 liters of volume, ideal for those more adventurous outings, while the daypack accommodates around 10 liters, excellent for daily essentials and little tech items.

The whole thing wears wonderfully thanks to smart straps and the clamshell opening makes loading and unloading super simple. It's tremendously durable and, as a perk to the artists out there, there's even camera cube integration, allowing you to neatly and safely stow all of your lenses and related gear. The shell is weatherproof and armed with theft-deterring pulls and, quite frankly, the bag looks cool as hell.

Essentially the volume of the pack, this is a crucial figure as it determines how much you can carry. Everyday packs tend to be on the smaller end (under 30 liters), but the exact number can determine whether you can sneak in that last change of clothes or extra water bottle comfortably.

A more technical figure, the dimensions are good to know for travel purposes. You want to know where the pack can fit in transit and also how big it might be when packed to the brim. These numbers can also give you a better idea of the fit of the pack, depending on the size of the wearer.

Will you be packing that computer? Most everyday packs account for that, with specialized sleeves and protective cubbies (some better than others). You'll want to know the details as some can handle bigger laptops or tablets than others, and some may require a sleeve or something extra to protect your machine. Some, of course, don't wish to travel with their computers and don't need the extra setup.

Will you be trekking into the elements? Walking through the rain in a pack that sticks out past your umbrella? Perhaps you're an all-weather cyclist commuter that needs some water resistance? This is an important feature if you plan to be outside in all seasons and carrying items (tech, for instance) that might not stand up to the precipitation as well.

While the weights of everyday packs do not differ a whole lot, a little can make a big difference if you're down a long hiking trail or wearing that pack all day for work. Extra weight can equate to more durability, but that's not always the case (and perhaps something you don't want if you have back issues or plan to be towing heavier loads).

Myself, along with MH editors, have tested dozens of backpacks over several months specifically for this buying guide, putting them through everyday use. That's a generic term, we know, but think morning commutes to work, bike rides to the store, weekend outings, field trips, journeys to the gym and back, and more. We tried them during a mix of activities with varied weights, sometimes just a pack of clothes or a water bottle on the way to the park, other times filled with books and a computer on a 20-mile bike ride.

In the end, we selected bags that were comfortable, functional, and offered deceptively helpful features. In addition to the above components, we analyzed online reviews, chatted up insiders on some of their favorite options, and looked for the newest and most improved packs from brands we've grown to respect and use ourselves.

#4684. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4683. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

#4682. 3 Insights If You're Looking for Love In Your "Golden Years"

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

The idea of finding love later in life might seem unconventional to some. In fact, one of the key misconceptions around aging is the belief that experiences of love and sexuality inevitably diminish with time.

Contrary to popular belief, many older adults continue to experience and seek romantic relationships well into their golden years, as you might have seen on ABC’s The Golden Bachelor. The need for companionship, emotional connection and intimacy remains fundamental to human well-being, regardless of age.

Here are three insights on love and sexuality in the golden years, according to research.

Research shows that for older individuals, a positive perception of sex and regular opportunities for sexual expression have been linked to physical and mental health benefits. However, this aspect of their lives tends to be overlooked or even dismissed by society.

A 2023 study found that older individuals may experience shame and guilt about discussing their sexuality with others due to the stigma they face. Participants reported that without these important conversations, they found it challenging to understand what is considered normal or “appropriate” sexual behavior for their age. They expressed a strong desire to live fully and to allow themselves to be seen as human beings with sexual needs.

Researchers highlighted the need for sexual health in older adults to be destigmatized. Discussions about sexual satisfaction are often redirected to potency-enhancing drugs by healthcare professionals rather than providing a much-needed space for older adults to express their sexual concerns, desires or fears.

As a society, we can all play a role in normalizing these conversations by challenging what aging means for one’s romantic and sexual life.

Finding love when older often involves a shift in priorities. Research shows that while dating online, younger adults tend to highlight themselves, their achievements, attractiveness and sexuality, older adults display more positive emotions, emphasizing the importance of emotional connection and health in their profiles.

In a 2021 study, most older adults showed interest in a fun-loving and compassionate partner. Further, older adult women sought partners who were honest and would engage in leisure activities with them, whereas older men were drawn to physically attractive and emotionally supportive partners.

Additionally, research highlights the importance of emotional safety, security and open communication in older adult relationships. For some older couples, sexual activities might occupy less space in the relationship and an emotional connection based on shared interests such as socializing with friends or traveling could take precedence.

Despite a decrease in such sexual spontaneity, many older individuals view this change positively. Planning sexual activities can become a deliberate choice, leading to partners prioritizing each other's pleasure, while also communicating about sexual expectations and concerns that arise with age-related physical changes.

It is important to acknowledge that aging brings unique challenges. Past traumas, health concerns and the loss of previous partners can cast shadows on the path to future romance. Widows and widowers, for example, may grapple with feelings of guilt or loyalty to a deceased spouse.

A 2022 study found that one’s perception of aging is influenced by transitions in and out of a marriage. Divorced or widowed individuals felt less positively about aging compared to those who stayed married. On the other hand, individuals who got married or entered a new marital relationship felt less negatively about aging than those who remained single.

Additionally, due to past experiences, many older adults are turning to cohabitation as an alternative to getting remarried. Research shows that there is no significant difference in relationship quality in both of these situations.

Research in 2020 found that older women in particular may not want to remarry and instead seek a companion with whom they can maintain their autonomy and financial independence, after years of likely having caregiving obligations.

Mature love, then, has various forms and involves a deep understanding of oneself and a lifetime of lessons. Past experiences can be transformed into wisdom and the resilience of the human spirit is evident in stories of seniors who, despite facing challenges, embrace the opportunity to love and be loved again.

The pursuit of love knows no age limit. The golden years present a unique and meaningful opportunity for seniors to rediscover the joys of romantic connection. With a lifetime of experiences to draw upon, the journey to finding love and embracing sexuality later in life can be a complex but rewarding experience.

#4681. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

#4680. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.
