#4679. Segway launches new electric motorcycle that’s so safe it has seatbelts

Segway came to EICMA this year with a surprisingly broad lineup of new electric motorcycles, ranging from high-performance concepts to off-road machines. But perhaps the most interesting of the bunch is also the one that looks the least like a conventional motorcycle or scooter.

Meet the Segway X Cruiser, an electric two-wheeler that takes motorcycle safety so seriously that it has a roll cage and seatbelts.

Or at least, those are among the configurations Segway is showing as it develops the new machine for production.

The X Cruiser is Segway’s attempt to bring more automotive-style protection to a single-track vehicle, essentially asking how much of a car’s safety envelope can be wrapped around a motorcycle without adding another pair of wheels.

From the looks of things, the answer is quite a lot.

Segway says the X Cruiser’s design was informed by automotive crash scenarios, with cage and semi-cage structures, four-direction collision protection, staged energy absorption, and seatbelt restraints intended to improve rider protection. It also gets active safety features including standard blind spot detection and lane change warning.

The company showed several ways that basic idea can be configured, ranging from a more conventional partially enclosed scooter-like setup to versions with significantly more structure surrounding the rider. One of the most striking configurations uses a heavily bolstered race-car-style seat and seatbelt along with protective framing around the rider, while another adds a roof for even more enclosure.

It’s a fascinating approach because motorcycles have traditionally relied largely on the rider wearing the protection. Helmets, jackets, gloves, boots and sometimes airbag vests form the safety system, while the motorcycle itself generally offers little physical protection during a crash.

The X Cruiser effectively flips part of that equation by building some of the protective structure into the vehicle itself.

There’s an important caveat here, though. Segway specifically notes that its descriptions refer to the vehicle’s current design and equipment and do not mean it has completed automotive-style crash certification. Final equipment and certification will depend on individual markets, so it sounds like the company is holding short of making any major certification claims. Still though, it’s easy to see how having what is effectively a racing seat and roll cage surrounding the rider could seriously contribute to better protection in a crash. Just remember to keep your hands and feet within the vehicle at all times.

And unlike plenty of wild EICMA showpieces, this one isn’t merely destined to live under convention-center spotlights. Segway says the X Cruiser has a confirmed mass-production plan, with launches planned for China and Europe between 2027 and 2028. There’s no US availability announcement yet.

Underneath all that protective hardware is a fairly serious electric touring platform. Segway is using its CTB (cell-to-body) battery integration to help improve structural rigidity and battery packaging, with the company targeting nearly 200 km (124 miles) of range.

European versions are expected to feature 4.5 kW Type 2 AC charging, while the Chinese version will offer optional higher-power DC fast charging. The bike rolls on 15-inch front and 14-inch rear wheels wearing Michelin City Grip tires, and riders get a 10.25-inch TFT display along with an optional 55-liter electrically operated top box.

Interestingly, the X Cruiser also incorporates certain two-wheeler intellectual property and know-how licensed from BMW Group, though Segway stresses that it is responsible for the vehicle’s development, integration, validation, production and certification.

The X Cruiser may be the weirdest – and thus perhaps the most interesting – of Segway’s EICMA debuts, but it was far from alone.

The company also unveiled the Segway Orca Concept, a futuristic high-performance electric maxi-scooter concept built around an 800V electrical architecture and a nearly 20 kWh battery.

Segway is targeting up to 300 km (186 miles) of range, a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) time of 4.5 seconds, and the ability to add 200 km (124 miles) of range in 20 minutes. The concept also features front and rear multi-link suspension, electronically controlled multi-mode damping and a battery-integrated CTB chassis. Those figures are engineering targets rather than promised production specifications, and Segway currently describes the Orca strictly as a concept.

Its a BMW C1 reborn as electric! They were a bit of a cult thing, but underpowered for the weight. Never made it to the USA.

The biggest benefit is not really safety, its comfort.

Then there’s Segway’s expanding X Series, which moves the focus away from urban riding and toward dirt. The lineup includes the Xaber X1000 and Xaber 350, along with different Xaber 300 variants for the US and European markets. Segway is also partnering with Michelin for its Dakar Rally Factory Team, using the brutal rally environment as a real-world development and validation platform for electric off-road motorcycles.

Taken together, it’s quite the showing from a company whose name many people still associate primarily with those funny two-wheeled self-balancing machines from the early 2000s.

Segway has already expanded heavily into electric scooters, e-bikes, go-karts and powersports vehicles. Now it seems increasingly serious about becoming an electric motorcycle company as well.

And if motorcycles with roll cages, roofs and seatbelts are part of that future, things could get pretty interesting… pretty quickly!

#4678. Can You Talk Your Way Into a Job?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Job interviews can feel overwhelming, but a 2024 study by Heimann & Schmitz-Wilemy suggests that being yourself may be the key to landing that job.

Research suggests that interviewees who are seen as more genuinely themselves are more likely to get the job. But do people who are more authentic during job interviews actually perform better at the job itself?

Researchers analyzed video recordings from 181 employed adults who participated in structured mock interviews and obtained job performance ratings from each participant’s supervisor. The study distinguished between verbal authenticity cues (what applicants say) and nonverbal authenticity cues (how they said it, including facial expressions, vocal style, and gestures).

Authenticity is that which makes us human. Think of authenticity cues as things a robot—or even artificial intelligence (AI)—is unlikely to do. Examples include expressing personal opinions, discussing personal topics from your private life (like whether a spouse is excited about this particular job opportunity), and talking about emotions in a way that feels sincere.

For example, “I’m excited by this job opportunity and know I can rise to the challenge,” or “I know I don’t have some of the experience you’re looking for, but I’m eager to learn”: The latter feels or sounds more like a human connection because of the acknowledgment of a weakness and the desire to overcome it.

Applicants who openly shared personal information, clearly stated their opinions, expressed emotions, and communicated in an expressive manner were more likely to be viewed as genuine and authentic by observers.

To determine whether an applicant's “realness” carries weight further than simply a first impression, the researchers controlled for observers' initial ratings of warmth and competence. Authenticity cues continued to predict (perceived) authenticity even after these factors were taken into account.

Our perception of someone being real with us in the moment is not entirely based on whether we think they are likeable or able to handle the job. Instead, we find ourselves subconsciously drawn to people who seem sincere. In sum, your foibles and flaws make you human. Yup, the way you stumbled a bit as you gave your answer or hesitated before responding to a question—that’s the part that makes you seem genuine, likeable, and, most importantly, management material.

Why aren’t we prizing perfect answers over genuine answers? Because gaining someone’s trust is crucial in the animal kingdom—and in the human kingdom as well.

We need to know who the predators are so that we don’t feel like prey, and I’m guessing that job interviewers are often suspicious that candidates are blowing smoke at them in an attempt to secure the job.

This study found that job interviewers paid particular attention to whether candidates expressed genuine opinions, shared their emotions (both good and bad), and communicated in a way that felt sincere.

Pretty well—but not for all people all the time.

Perceived authenticity predicted who was most likely to get hired, but researchers also predicted that authenticity cues displayed during interviews would be associated with supervisor ratings of job performance.

But it turns out that this prediction was only partially supported.

Verbal authenticity cues showed a significant positive relationship with supervisor-rated job performance (r = .24), whereas nonverbal authenticity cues did not show a significant relationship (r = .09).

In other words, applicants who clearly expressed their opinions, discussed emotions, and avoided vague or superficial responses tended to perform better at work according to their supervisors. The superficial acts of appearing expressive, animated, or engaging through nonverbal behavior were not associated with better job performance.

There were three verbal behaviors that were important when it came to job performance: clearly stating personal opinions, providing specific rather than vague responses, and discussing emotions when appropriate. The idea is that clear, direct interaction is helpful in both a job interview and in facilitating effective work relationships. Effective work relationships with open and honest communication are more likely to result in a secure and successful work environment. When employees are happy and feel supported by management, their employment goals are more likely to be met, and their bosses are more likely to approve of their leadership skills.

Don’t be a robot during a job interview; just be yourself. Stop obsessing over the “right” answer to a question and go for the truth: I’m not perfect, but I’m always looking to improve. And use your real-life language and wording, not something you copied out of a manual or learned from your AI best friend. It appears that either consciously or subconsciously, interviewers respond not only to your on-paper qualifications but also to you as a person.

Heimann, A.L., Schmitz-Wilhelmy, A. Observing Interviewees’ Inner Self: How Authenticity Cues in Job Interviews Relate to Interview and Job Performance. J Bus Psychol 40, 237–256 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-024-09949-4

BYD launched the new Seal 07 in China, where it starts at around $23,000. It’s about the size of a Toyota Camry, but brings a surprising amount of tech and premium features for the money.

After introducing the updated first-generation Seal 07 in March, BYD launched the second-gen model on Thursday.

The second-generation Seal 07, which BYD calls the “new choice for a class-leading luxury experience,” is available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains.

BYD offers five variants, including two PHEVs and three EVs, starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery, providing a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

Higher-priced models offer BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, with a roof-mounted LiDAR available as an option. The setup provides safety and convenience features such as Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

BYD is offering a limited-time “Super trade-in price” promo, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

#4676. Tesla wants its sworn Cybercab answers to NHTSA kept entirely secret

Tesla has answered NHTSA’s Special Order demanding it prove, under oath, that the Cybercab meets federal safety standards. The response landed on the October 30 deadline, and Tesla asked the agency to keep all of it confidential.

The only part of the filing the public can read is a 30-page guide for firefighters. Everything about how a car with no steering wheel, pedals, or mirrors was certified as compliant is blacked out.

We reported in September that NHTSA had ordered Tesla to show its work on the Cybercab’s certification. The order came one week after the company started charging for Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3 and put 21 questions to the company, with civil penalties of up to $139 million for an incomplete answer and criminal exposure for a false one.

Tesla first tried to buy time. On September 18, it asked for eight more weeks, until November 20, citing “the voluminous nature of the request” and the work of searching its records and writing “thorough narrative formats in response to each question.” NHTSA gave it 30 days instead. The new deadline was October 30, and Tesla met it.

Three Tesla documents now sit in the AQ26002 docket, and two of them are empty.

The first is Tesla’s response letter, dated October 30 and addressed from 1 Tesla Road in Austin. It is one page long. The only text is: “The entirety of this file is confidential business information.”

The second is a placeholder for Tesla’s answer to Request 8, which asked the company to explain, standard by standard, how it determined the Cybercab complies: which subpart it certified to, and whether it ran physical tests, simulations, or engineering analyses. Per NHTSA’s note, the responsive documents carry a confidentiality request “for the entirety of each document.”

The third is the only substantive document: Tesla’s Cybercab First Responder Interaction Plan, version 1.2, dated September 3. It’s a real document with useful information in it. It’s also something Tesla has had on its website since July, aimed at police and fire crews, not regulators.

So the public gets a tow-truck manual, and the certification argument stays sealed.

The Special Order wasn’t a fishing expedition. It named the rules the Cybercab doesn’t obviously meet, and it seeks to understand how Tesla believes it can get around it.

FMVSS 135 says “the service brakes shall be activated by means of a foot control.” NHTSA has stated in public that a manufacturer of a vehicle with no foot brake can’t certify to it, then asked Tesla how it did. FMVSS 108 requires a turn-signal control that cancels itself when the steering wheel turns. FMVSS 111 requires mirrors. And the agency wanted to know whether Tesla certified the car with temporary driver controls bolted in and then removed them, which would run into the Safety Act’s “make inoperative” prohibition.

It also asked how the Cybercab is legal without a Part 555 exemption, the route Amazon’s Zoox took for its own steering-wheel-less robotaxi in July. Zoox applied, made its case, and got an exemption capped at 2,500 vehicles a year. Tesla self-certified and started charging for rides.

Every one of those answers is now under a confidentiality claim.

The first-responder plan was written for a different audience, but it brushes against several of NHTSA’s questions.

It says the Cybercab is “not typically equipped with a steering wheel or acceleration and brake pedals.” The word “typically” is doing work there. The same document notes that a Cybercab with a steering wheel and pedals “is typically an engineering or test vehicle, and operates at SAE Level 2 autonomy,” and includes instructions for driving one. That’s relevant to Requests 5 through 7, which asked whether the subject vehicles can be driven with temporarily attached controls.

It describes an operational design domain covering “all public roadways, such as freeways, highways, city streets, and rural roads,” at all hours, in light and moderate rain, fog, and snow. That is a far wider envelope than the Austin geofence the cars run in today, and it references an “Arizona Areas of Operation Appendix.” Request 1 asked for the ODD and Request 2 for scaling plans.

And it confirms that first responders can be granted access to on-board touchscreen controls to move the car, after showing a badge to the B-pillar camera (that’s interesting). Request 20 asked whether the touchscreen can move the vehicle and under what restrictions.

Nothing in it touches brakes, mirrors, telltales, or the certification itself.

Confidentiality requests go to NHTSA’s Chief Counsel under Part 512. The agency decides whether Tesla’s claim holds, and it can order a public version released if it doesn’t. NHTSA hasn’t said anything about the request, and it hasn’t found the Cybercab noncompliant with any standard.

This is familiar. In June 2025, Tesla asked NHTSA to hide its answers about the original Robotaxi launch in Austin, a service running on supervised FSD while FSD was under investigation. Those answers never surfaced.

NHTSA’s opening resume for the audit put the affected population at about 1,000 vehicles. The Cybercab is still carrying passengers in Austin while the agency reads a filing nobody else can.

I don't see how the answers can have confidential business secrets. It is about meeting public safety standards, not asking for schematics, technical details or designs. It is about clear public safety requirement and how the vehicle qualify as meeting it.

The so called keyword from Tesla's self certification is "applicable". Tesla may argue that many of those requirements aren't applicable in their test vehicle. But I would like to see the justifications on that.

Tesla’s position in September was that the Cybercab complies with every applicable federal standard, including the one that requires a brake pedal. If that’s true, the argument for it is the most interesting document in the autonomous vehicle industry right now, and Tesla just asked the government to make sure nobody reads it.

We get why a company redacts test data and supplier details. But the legal theory for how a car with no foot brake meets a foot-brake rule doesn’t sound like a trade secret to me. Zoox’s exemption petition is public. Waymo’s safety framework is public. Tesla’s case for why it didn’t need to ask is sealed, cover letter included.

NHTSA now has to decide whether “the entirety of this file” is really confidential business information. If it says no, we’ll finally see how Tesla certified this car. If it says yes, about 1,000 Cybercabs keep driving on a certification the public isn’t allowed to check.

A robotaxi that only runs when the grid is up is a reminder that electricity is the one fuel cost you can actually control at home. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. It’s a free service with hundreds of pre-vetted installers competing for your business, so you save 20 to 30% compared to going it alone. No sales calls until you pick an installer. #4675. A Healthy Animal Can Still Be Miserable

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Animal welfare has a long history of disregard. In early Western philosophy, Aristotle argued that animals lacked moral status as they lacked the capacity to reason, and this tradition continued through to the Cartesian perspective of animals as automata that lacked mental states. This view has now been largely overturned in favour of one that recognises animals as sentient creatures with moral value. Indeed, during recent decades, animal welfare has also become a scientific discipline of its own. The difficulty of measuring animal welfare, however, can still be vastly underestimated.

Scientific investigation is always relative to some perspective. Scientists have different perspectives, arising from their background theories and the capabilities of their measurement instruments, each of which can reveal only a partial view of the objects under investigation. Given that no single perspective can offer a uniquely correct and complete picture of the world, use of multiple perspectives together can thus create a far richer understanding. Different methods and models offer different perspectives and ways of gaining knowledge.

After all, it is only rarely, if ever, the case that much can be learned by a single method, experiment, or measurement: science requires pluralism and diversity even on the lowest scale. Animal welfare is a complex concept, of which there are multiple theoretical perspectives and associated different measurement methods, each with differing strengths and weaknesses and which shed light on different aspects of the phenomenon of welfare. As I shall show, this diversity is to be embraced, rather than avoided.

The three primary views are what Green and Mellor describe as the ‘three orientations’: biological function, natural living, and affective state.

The biological function perspective focuses on the physical wellbeing of an animal. An animal can be entirely fit and healthy, but still feel bored, lonely and frustrated, and thus have poor welfare.

The natural living perspective focuses on the wild state of animals and their ability to function according to how they have been shaped by evolution. The natural living perspective has been criticized for its limitations, as many aspects of the ‘natural’ lives of animals (i.e. those experienced in the wild) can be detrimental to welfare (e.g. predation, disease). An animal can be living a perfectly natural life, but suffer immensely from these effects.

The affective state perspective takes welfare to consist in the mental states, or affects, of animals and is also often known as the ‘feelings-based’ approach. Positive feelings (such as comfort or curiosity) increase welfare, while negative feelings (such as hunger or pain) decrease welfare. Under almost all conceptions, the feelings of animals, their pleasure and suffering, are central to considerations of welfare. As such, the affective state perspective is now commonly accepted as necessary for welfare. However, it is often considered insufficient. An animal may experience nothing but happiness lying around eating chocolate, but the resulting health compromise will lead to poor welfare.

Welfare is complex, and thus no single theory will provide sufficient information about all its parts.

There are numerous measures for animal welfare, which can be grouped as physical, behavioural and environmental. Cortisol is a hormone associated with the stress response, and so elevated levels can indicate the presence of stress and possible corresponding reduction in welfare. Stereotypies are repetitive behaviours such as pacing, swaying, or self-plucking and their presence is typically assumed to signal boredom or frustration, where an animal is unable to perform a highly motivated behaviour and instead redirects its energies into the observed unnatural stereotypy.

Any single measure on its own will not provide much information about welfare; like a single torch, it will only light up one small part of the whole.

Using multiple measures alongside one another will allow us to gain the benefits of each method, while offsetting their drawbacks. For example, if we failed to include an indicator for social behaviour in a highly social animal held in a solitary environment, we might conclude that welfare was good, even though an important component of natural behaviour is missing.

Another related concern regarding the risks in bringing together multiple perspectives and measurements for a pluralist study of animal welfare is that the measures and recommendations arising from each may conflict. For example, many zoos used to have concrete and tiled cages, which allowed for maximising welfare from a physical functioning perspective, through thorough cleaning and disinfecting. However, the lack of environmental complexity and mental stimulation detracted from welfare from both the natural living and affective state perspectives.

It is important, when adopting a plurality of perspectives, to ensure that there is a way of adjudicating between their competing demands and setting weightings between the different components. However, there is no ‘objective’ or ‘perspective-neutral’ viewpoint from which to assess the weightings of various inputs.

Regardless, these concerns do not make integration an unachievable task. In making animal welfare assessments, our purposes are typically for making decisions about where best to use our resources to maximise welfare. Here, I might consider using robustness reasoning. This would entail comparing the decisions recommended by different models, and preferentially selecting those recommended by many or most models. In practice, often the recommendations from the different welfare perspectives align, and so this should not be excessively demanding.

Animal welfare is real and measurable, and although incredibly complex, no less so than its human counterpart. I hope that the foregoing analysis has demonstrated a way to partially escape the limited human perspective via the use of a plurality of diverse methods to explore a complex phenomenon.

If you enjoyed this essay, you might enjoy the academic article on which it is based.

Veit, W., & Browning, H. (2021). Perspectival pluralism for animal welfare. European Journal for Philosophy of Science, 11, 9. Download

#4674. Hyundai is recalling nearly 30,000 Kona Electric vehicles due to an airbag software defect

Hyundai issued a recall affecting nearly 30,000 Kona Electric vehicles due to a software error that could cause the airbag to fail to deploy in a crash.

In a letter sent to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on November 4, Hyundai said it was recalling certain 2019 to 2023 Kona Electric and 2019 to 2022 Veloster N vehicles.

The recall impacts 37,901 vehicles in total, including 29,058 Kona Electric and 8,843 Veloster N models.

According to documents submitted to the NHTSA, the issue stems from a software error with the airbag control unit (ACU) that can cause the airbag malfunction indicator light (MIL) to come on and the airbag system to deactivate under certain driving conditions.

The data may become corrupted during a system reboot or power interruption while the system is writing to the ACU’s memory. When this happens, the airbag MIL will illuminate to warn drivers.

As of October 22, 2026, Hyundai is aware of 331 alleged incidents related to the issue. However, none have resulted in a crash, fire, or injury.

Owners can take their vehicle to the closest dealer, where it will update the ACU software, free of charge.

Hyundai expects to mail out owner notification letters on January 1, 2027. In the meantime, owners can contact Hyundai’s customer service at 1-855-371-9460 with any questions or concerns. Hyundai’s recall number is 311.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the NHTSA.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V728.

#4673. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4672. Be the Riverbank for Children’s Emotional Rivers

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

“I used to yell at my daughter when she cried, to make her tougher. Even after I learned that crying is how she expresses herself when she has big emotions, I still yelled. I couldn’t deal with feeling helpless to make her happy again. Slowly, I learned that I have to take care of my own emotions and let my own tears out. Now when my daughter cries I cuddle with her, she lets out her tears, and we both feel better afterward. We call it cuddling the cry away.”

Children’s emotions need to flow freely, like a river. That means parents need to be the riverbank. A riverbank safely contains the flow of feelings—preventing a flood—but doesn’t dam the flow by ignoring feelings, judging them, or forcing them to change. After all, a riverbank doesn’t decide how warm or cool the water in the river should be, or how fast or slow it should flow.

Parents who can express their own emotions in a healthy way can listen to children’s feelings without becoming overwhelmed by them. As a dad said to me recently, “I often tell my children something that I only learned recently for myself: If you are happy, you can laugh; if you are sad, you can cry.”

The riverbank is the river’s home. Children need a safe physical home, and they also need a safe emotional home, often called the secure home base. This isn’t always easy for adults. It’s hard to sit with intense feelings in children, especially difficult ones like anger or grief.

Imagine two children who fight at a playground, and each goes running to their parent. One parent says, “Don’t come crying to me.” The other parent says, “Oh, poor baby, we will never come to this playground again. I’ll never let that mean child near you.” I see many instances of each extreme—dismissal of the child’s emotions or joining the child in emotional flooding.

In between is a good level of emotional support: “That looked like it hurt your body and your feelings. How did you try to solve the problem? How did that work? What else might you try next?”

If you can talk with both children, you might add: “Looks like you two are having some trouble. It’s hard when friends fight. Does anyone have any ideas on how to play together again?”

Children need a safe place for the free flow of all their feelings, but a safe home base is especially relevant for sadness. When children feel sadness, loneliness, or loss, they need a place of warmth and love where they can heal from that pain.

Mabel was almost 3 when her parents began to talk to her about starting preschool. It would be her first time away from both parents for any extended period. She enjoyed her visit to the school, but asked her mother many times, “Will you be here with me?” When she understood that she would not be with her parents or grandparents at school, she lost her enthusiasm and was a bit sad.

Mabel’s family understood that their job was to offer comfort and security, not to convince her it would be fun: “I understand that you’re sad. It’s hard to imagine having fun when you’ll miss your family.”

A few days before school started, while her grandma gave her a bath, Mabel said to the little bath-toy animals, “You’re going to school.” Grandma picked up a toy and gave it a voice: “Will you be with me?” Mabel answered, taking on the role of the mother, “You’ll be by yourself.” Grandma had her animal say with worry, “Oh no!” Mabel responded gently, “Oh, it will be OK.” Then they made all the animals splash around in the water, with lots of laughter.

This game provided Mabel with the ability to work through her sad feelings, and she made an excellent adjustment to preschool. Of course, she was sad sometimes when saying goodbye, but she knew she had a safe place at home to feel her sadness.

It is inevitable that children will be sad at times. Children need to know that their parents can handle their heartbreak, without becoming so overwhelmed that they respond with anger or dismissal, such as: “Stop crying or I’ll leave you here all alone.” Sad children need to hear instead, “I’m here with you. This is very painful. Together we can hold this big feeling.” This may not make the sadness go away immediately. That’s not the goal. A mother confronted me at a workshop: “I listened to my son, like you said, and he was still sad.” Yes, it’s heartbreaking and true. Fortunately, it’s not a parent’s job to take away the feeling, but to sit with the child while the tears flow. The sadness will pass.

A mother recently shared with me an example of this new way of thinking about sadness:

“The other day my daughter came back from the neighbor’s house crying. The other children did not play with her, and she felt very sad. I squatted down and hugged her. At the same time, my brain was thinking fast. How should I solve the problem for her? For a moment, I had nothing to say, so I repeated what she told me and looked at her. I gave her a hug and sympathized with her. She finished her tears and had good ideas for resolving these friendship issues the next time. The trouble was solved easily. Our emotional connection worked much better than my usual approach, which was to tell her what she should do. In this case, it was a very good thing that I couldn’t think of any so-called good ideas!”

It is time to stop seeing tears as a sign of weakness, especially in boys, who are expected to be tough from the very start of their lives. Many boys learn the “boy rules” and try to block all their tears from an early age. If they are “successful,” they are on the road to being emotionally constricted men. If they “fail,” they may be teased or bullied by other boys, or even by adults. This puts boys in an impossible position. The solution is for them to have safety at home, with parents, to let down their guard and let out their tears, even if they choose to hold them in sometimes with their peers. Boys are lucky if they know that someone sees them as OK no matter what they feel or how they show it. Boys are really lucky if they have adult men in their lives who are willing to accept tears, talk about emotions, and even cry themselves sometimes.

Children’s sadness needs to flow freely, with a loving adult sitting nearby or holding them close. Even the toughest kids (and grownups) have tears inside that need to come out.

WHETHER YOU'RE A grooming editor, like me, whose skincare routine is extensive (and seemingly growing every day), or a bare-minimum type of guy, your regimen centers on the same thing: moisturizer. After the face wash, serum, and eye cream, applying moisturizer brings it all home. The only product that should follow is sunscreen in the morning (year-round, please!), so it’s crucial to find one you dig that matches your skin type and budget.

For those who are especially short on time or stubborn about keeping their skincare routine short, there are plenty of quality SPF moisturizers to consider. Regardless, moisturizer is the crux of proper skincare. The third act climax that culminates the impact of all that has preceded it and cements a lingering effect of what follows.

Applying twice a day (once in the morning, once at night) strengthens your skin barrier, locks in hydration, and keeps your complexion healthy and balanced. Of course, not all moisturizers are created equal, and few are effective for all skin types. These are the best available for everybody’s skin.

Neutrogena’s Hydro Boost Face Moisturizer has been in rotation for dermatologist Dr. Alex Zeitany, M.D., since 2015—and it’s the one she consistently recommends to patients looking for serious hydration without the heavy feel. Powered by hyaluronic acid, which holds up to 1,000 times its weight in water, this gel delivers a cool, weightless finish while locking in moisture like a pro, according to Dr. Zeitany.

I’ve applied this before heading out into serious heat (followed by sunscreen, of course), and my skin was never dry or tight, remaining smooth and hydrated for hours. Add in the fact that it could double as the best budget moisturizer at barely over $25, and it’s hard to find a reason against this ultra-hydrating option.

Testing Notes: Like many men, I tend to shy away from moisturizers that leave my skin feeling goopy or greasy, which is why this watery gel rose to the top of the list. It glides onto skin easily and has a slight cooling sensation, but also sinks into your skin quickly without leaving any sort of shine or residue whatsoever.

The formula is packed with hyaluronic acid, one of the most important ingredients in a moisturizer because it is a humectant—meaning it draws moisture from the air—and even with a formula as lightweight as this, my skin still felt healthy and hydrated hours later.

You don't need a moisturizer to be 100 percent natural or organic to be effective—some of the most proven skincare ingredients, including ceramides (barrier repair), niacinamide (brightening and redness reduction), glycerin (hydration), and hyaluronic acid (moisture retention), are often lab-made and highly effective at supporting healthy, hydrated skin. But if your skin tends to appreciate more natural formulas, or you want something a bit more environmentally friendly, Jackfir is the ideal choice.

According to dermatologist Dr. Joshua Zeichner, M.D., moisturizers primarily rely on three types of ingredients: occlusives, humectants, and emollients. Your skin type determines which you should zero in on. They break down like this.

As a grooming editor, I am constantly testing moisturizers, including the latest innovations and releases. I have normal to dry skin, which can also be quite sensitive and prone to acne, so I’m able to test a wide range of moisturizers for most skin types other than oily. In fact, I write a bi-monthly column detailing my favorite new releases in grooming across all categories, and moisturizers often make the cut. For this story, I collected a group of my all-time favorites, past and present, to reevaluate over the past year-plus on their ingredients, feel, consistency, and long-term effectiveness.

That being said, I am far from the only one at Men’s Health who takes skincare seriously (our office is like #boybathroom gone wild). I also considered the go-to picks of fellow editors and writers, who have been testing moisturizers since our grooming vertical first launched in 2018. I especially considered recommendations for those with oily skin, to cover all skin type bases.

Finally, I presented the extensive list of moisturizers that saw positive results to a panel of dermatologists to ensure every entry was effective and safe, while inquiring about which they recommend to their patients. With all this in mind, I narrowed our list to the ten best moisturizers for men with any skin type, be it dry, oily, sensitive, or somewhere in between.

Men need to moisturize every day—full stop. This is regardless of skin type, as even oily and acne-prone skin needs the added benefits of a moisturizing product to help regulate sebum production, according to dermatologist Dr. Corey L. Hartman, M.D. No matter your skin type, you should apply a moisturizer twice daily—once in the morning and once at night.

Moisturizer should always be the last or second-to-last step in your routine. They’re designed to not only impart hydration to your skin but also lock in the moisture that it already has, as well as the ingredients in any other products you’ve used.

An easy way to remember it is this: No matter how many products you’re using, you want to layer them from thinnest to thickest textures. After cleansing, apply any serums or other thinner products before sealing them all in with your moisturizer. In the morning, you’ll want to top the moisturizer with sunscreen, but at night, you can just end with your moisturizer.

A lot of guys skip moisturizing because they hate how it feels—greasy, heavy, or sticky formulas are instant dealbreakers. The good news? Moisturizers come in all forms, including gels, which pack high water content for fast absorption and a clean, non-tacky finish, according to dermatologist Dr. Estee Williams, M.D.

Your choice should match your skin type—gels work best for oily skin, while thicker creams suit dry patches—but the key is picking a moisturizer you actually want to use every day. If it’s just gathering dust on your shelf, it’s doing nothing for your skin.

Dermatologist Dr. Sarah Stierman, M.D., recommends using multi-tasking moisturizers that include niacinamide, which fights inflammation and prevents blemishes in oily skin; hyaluronic acid, which attracts and locks in moisture; and ceramides, which repair the skin barrier and soothe the skin, crucial for anyone who shaves regularly.

#4669. Meta-backed 250 MW solar farm breaks ground in Arkansas

Arkansas is getting another 250 megawatts (MW) of solar power, and Meta has signed up to buy it.

EDP Renewables North America (EDPR NA) broke ground on Cypress Knee Solar in Chicot County, in the southeastern corner of the state, on November 4. The solar farm is expected to be completed by 2028, bringing several hundred construction jobs and an estimated $25 million in county revenue over its lifetime.

Meta’s long-term power purchase agreement helps it work toward its pledge to match 100% of its annual electricity use with renewable energy generation. Don’t confuse that pledge with Meta powering its data centers with renewables around the clock, though – Facebook and Instagram’s parent company is also backing new gas plants to meet its growing power demand.

The companies announced the deal in May. Cypress Knee is their third clean-energy agreement, bringing the total capacity covered by Meta’s deals with EDPR NA to 545 MW.

“As energy demand continues to rise, projects like Cypress Knee Solar help strengthen grid reliability while creating jobs, generating meaningful local revenue, and delivering long-term benefits to the communities that host them,” said EDPR NA CEO Sandhya Ganapathy.

EDPR NA says it has already contributed more than $77,000 during project development, including money to restore the Lakeside High School greenhouse, resources for the Lakeside Robotics team, and funding for the Lake Village food pantry.

#4668. What Your Doctor Fails to Tell You Can Definitely Hurt

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

When you think about your physical health, it’s natural to think of all the ways a physician or similar healthcare provider should be able to help you. If you or a loved one have developed a chronic disease that requires monitoring, surgery, or a switch in medications, you’ll probably feel that this is enough to get things back on track on the road to recovery.

As it turns out, a number of medical conditions and treatments have important psychological connections that are equally important to promote healing. Whether it’s depression, cognitive changes, or anxiety, you may not realize that these are natural outcomes of various types of interventions. Unfortunately, healthcare professionals aren’t always either (a) aware of these connections or (b) prepared (or have the time) to address them.

In a review of studies “at the intersection of psychiatry and cardiology,” Medical University of Silesia’s Kamila Klimek-Ociepka and colleagues scanned various databases to identify publications over the 15-year period of 2010 to 2025 in which findings were reported on the conjunction of cardiac device implantation (such as pacemakers) and assessment of patient symptoms in the domains of depression, anxiety, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and cognitive disorders. A total of 44 studies made it to the final set used to analyze the main findings.

Key to understanding these studies is “heart-focused anxiety (HFA).” As you might imagine, having a procedure done to your heart, even if it is meant to reduce your risk of dying, is hardly a minor episode in your life. Anxiety and depression are reported in as many as 44 percent of patients treated with internal devices meant to keep the heart beating regularly.

In particular, HFA occurs when people experience “excessive anxiety related specifically to cardiac sensations, symptoms, and anticipated cardiovascular events.” People with certain types of implants, the ones that perform internal defibrillation (to get the heart started, are particularly likely to have HFA, fearing being harmed by the voltage from the shocks the device performs. Instead of engaging in what would be heart-healthy exercise, they instead decide they could hurt themselves by making the heart overwork, leading to an actual worsening of their condition.

Depressive symptoms, for their part, can also become highly prevalent among cardiac patients, with estimates ranging up to 64 percent, especially when they first learn of their diagnosis. Their depression can be expressed as sleep disturbances and loss of energy, or in the emotional realm as hopelessness and pessimism about the future.

Finally, PTSD can also develop in patients who experienced sudden cardiac events or invasive therapies. There are probably few traumas that can occur in daily life as frightening as having your heart literally stop for a second or two. But because they don’t remember the event, their PTSD may be expressed as “hypervigilance, anxiety, and avoidance behaviors rather than intrusive memories or flashbacks.”

In reading about these psychological consequences of cardiac events and treatment, you might be wondering why you’ve never heard anyone speak about them in the context of treatment. Shouldn’t you (or your relative) have been warned or at least educated about these risks? Considering all the precautions listed on any kind of medical consent form, you would think that it might be worth adding these—along with an explanation.

Additionally, as pointed out by Erzurum Bolge Training and Research Hospital's Murat Özmen, physicians may not realize that depression can be associated with the low physical activity, high stress, obesity, and hypertension that are part of the disease picture. Just as physicians and other healthcare professionals instruct their patients about implanted devices themselves, the authors claim they need to educate them about the importance of sleep, developing coping methods to reduce stress, and participating in exercise as warranted by stage of recovery.

The experience of cardiovascular disease is clearly life-threatening and scary, but even more ominous is a diagnosis of cancer. Considering how highly prevalent cancer is within the population, it’s likely that someone you know (or you) has received this diagnosis.

It may seem almost self-evident that the uncertainty of a cancer diagnosis, along with the stress involved in tests, procedures, and therapy, would be enough to lead a patient’s mind to travel to existential questions about the possibility of surviving into the future. Fortunately, those who treat cancer patients are tuned in to the psychological risks. University of Houston’s Haejeong An and Yoonjung Kim note that this “general understanding is expanded by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), which specifically defines distress as a multifaceted concept covering physical, psychological, social, or spiritual discomfort that emerges during cancer survivorship, which affects how survivors think, feel, or act.”

Unfortunately, though, the concept of distress is not well-defined in actual practice. Therapeutic approaches fail to separate distress from anxiety, depression, and stress, meaning that interventions will fail to target this piece of the cancer journey separately and effectively. Starting with a database of more than 2,700 studies, the authors analyzed the final 14 that met all the rigorous criteria for inclusion.

The methods used in these studies were all over the map, ranging from standard psychological interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to virtual reality, mindfulness, and hypnosis. As a result, there were inconsistent findings regarding effectiveness, a problem made worse by lack of a clear definition of distress.

Compared to cardiac disease, the scope of psychosocial interventions for cancer patients is far more advanced. However, the U. Houston findings suggest that practitioners do not have clear pathways for reducing the distress of their patients, if they indeed decide to implement some type of intervention.

These examples of research in the area of psychological symptoms and serious disease should alert you to the idea that if you (or a loved one) are headed for some type of intervention, it’s important to be aware of possible emotional consequences. In an era of overburdened healthcare providers, where you may feel lucky to get an appointment at all, finding ways to receive this support may seem impossible.

However, if it’s not from the provider itself, consider seeking support from other sources. There is a wide number of support groups associated with specific diseases, but if there isn’t one in your community, you can also draw from online resources. You can even start your own group.

An added piece of irony in the equation is that behavioral medicine often focuses on ways to help patients adopt healthier lifestyles. Less often does the field seek connections between physical disease and mental health. The An and Kim article suggests some causes of optimism given the large number of intervention studies in the area of breast cancer. The problem in this area is not lack of recognition, but lack of definitions and clear methodologies, leading to the exclusion of most available research.

To sum up, the next time you draw up your list of questions to ask your healthcare provider before going in for an appointment, think about whether your stress, anxiety, and depression might also be important to mention. Your mental health and your physical health can only stand to gain.

Klimek-Ociepka, K., Kruczaj, K., Dyrbuś, M., Pudlo, R., Gąsior, M., & Tajstra, M. (2026). At the Intersection of Psychiatry and Cardiology: Assessment of Depressive, Anxiety and Cognitive Disorders in Patients Before and After the Implantation of Cardiac Implantable Electronic Devices. Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania), 62(7), 1255. https://doi.org/10.3390/medicina62071255

Özmen, M., Altunkaya, O., Aydemir, S., Aydın, S. Ş., Aydınyılmaz, F., Aksakal, E., & Alkan, E. (2025). Evaluatıon of Depressıon and Anxıety Status in Patıents After Cardıac Devıce Implantatıon. Annals of Noninvasive Electrocardiology, 30(3), e70085. https://doi.org/10.1111/anec.70085

An, H., & Kim, Y. (2025). Managing psychological distress in women with breast cancer: A systematic review of intervention trends in the past decade. Asia-Pacific Journal of Oncology Nursing, 13, 100826. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apjon.2025.100826

#4667. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

It has already been a big part of Kia’s comeback in China and is expected to become one of its best-selling EVs.

Kia appears to be preparing an updated version. A new EV5 model was recently spotted by ShortsCar in a South Korean parking garage without camouflage, and it’s expected to be the updated version.

You can see in the video that the design has changed quite a bit. Up front, the hood and headlights remain about the same, but new design elements like a black accent light are added.

It also features a unique bumper design, similar to that of the rugged EV5 WKNDR Concept Kia revealed last November at the Guangzhou Motor Show.

The biggest changes are inside, where the interior appears to be completely overhauled. Instead of the current large display screen spanning from the driver to the center, the new EV5 features a display that extends from the center to the passenger side.

There also appears to be an added slim display in front of the steering wheel. Since Hyundai has recently added a slim display to vehicles equipped with its Pleos infotainment system, the updated Kia EV5 is expected to feature the new setup.

However, this is still speculation and has not been confirmed. The center console has also changed. Instead of the physical buttons, it now has a cover, giving it a cleaner overall look.

According to a sticker on the back, the updated EV5 is set to launch in the Philippines. Given Kia initially launched the EV5 in China in 2023, it will be due for a facelift around 2027.

Kia has yet to confirm whether and when it will launch the updated EV5 in other global markets, such as Europe or Korea. It will likely arrive after the China-made version, like the current EV5. We should learn more details soon.

#4665. What's in a Label With Neurodivergence, and Why You Should Care

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Recently, I was having coffee with a few colleagues when the topic of labels came up. One of our clients said they self-identified as an “autistic person" versus a "neurodivergent person." This is a distinction worth noting since neurodivergence can be viewed as a broad term. Everyone's eyes turned to me in anticipation of my response because, of course, I'm known around the office for having what my children call "hot takes." Without hesitation, I shared mine: "I support specific labels across the neurodivergent community, as long as they don't define an individual's entire identity." My team was divided, but let me explain my stance.

As someone who's part of Generation X, when I was a child, there were far fewer labels. No one was diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or learning disabilities. If there was an academic challenge, the kids figured it out or didn’t. As for me, I was a fun, fearless, and resilient child. No one told me who I was, and I embraced that way of thinking, often finding solutions along the way. Fast forward to today, this isn't the case at all in any aspect of our society. Labels are a way people identify themselves, especially those within the neurodivergent community. And within these labels, there is identity-first language and person-centered language, which we've touched on in the past. See here for more background if you’re too busy to scan through my previous blog posts.

These terms aside, if you're not working in the field like me, and labeling your child makes you uncomfortable, that's a good thing. It means you're thoughtful and sensitive. But I'll be clear: A label stating an actual diagnosis is imperative. In my line of work, I create programs for people with disabilities, and many clients have ADHD and/or autism. I often find myself using a label to support client advocacy and secure supports. In cases like this one, a label is vital. If a client doesn't have a formal diagnosis of autism, they might not receive services from a school system, disability development services, or health insurance. For them, the lack of a label means no consideration for applied behavior analysis (ABA) therapy; the answer is simply "no."

Over the years, I've met many clients who proudly share their diagnosis: "This is who I am, and accept me for me." They identify with a label because it helps them explain how they differ from the general population, and, in some cases, that label becomes a central part of their identity. This is where it can get tricky.

One strong example is Asperger's syndrome, once a widely used diagnosis, which has largely faded from everyday use and has been absorbed into the diagnosis of autism. Many people with Asperger's still use the term and feel that the shift erases part of themselves and others' history. Without a distinct category, their needs may even be overlooked. Some believe they’ve lost a sense of self, and I really feel for them. I can't imagine someone telling me something I've connected to for years essentially no longer exists.

A great way to find a healthy balance when approaching labels within neurodivergence is to find a community of people who share your child's background. When integrating, your child will likely see that, yes, they share a label and some similarities, but they have their own unique personality and interests. This realization can also help a child who might feel isolated by fostering connections.

At the end of the day, every person is an individual, and yes, labels are a necessary part of life and play a huge role in our healthcare system. However, again, I'm not the one labeling my clients; I ask them to tell me, and if that's challenging, I work with their parent or caregiver for insight. Ask, don't assume.

After working for so many years with families with children with disabilities, I can assure you that as a parent, you can deeply impact the way your child sees themselves and trust and believe they're so much more than the label they might currently identify with. Encourage them to accept who they are, know that they bring something special to the world, and continue to find the wonderful qualities and characteristics that go far beyond a label because that's what makes them special and unique. The diagnosis is just one part of who they are. I know my younger self would be shocked by my new acceptance of labels, but she was never defined by one thing, and neither is your child.

#4664. The Best Men's Travel Blazers in 2026, Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Silhouettes from Uniqlo, Suitsupply, and Eddie Bauer went the distance in our testing.

WHETHER YOU’RE PACKING for a trip or just gearing up for a long commute, keeping a travel blazer in your rotation saves you time—and a lot of outfit stress. When you’re bouncing from one to the next with no time to reset, this is the one piece in your wardrobe that won’t fall apart. Unlike traditional blazers, these travel styles resist wrinkles, breathe easily, and have enough stretch that you still feel comfortable during those cramped flights and shoulder-to-shoulder train rides. On top of that, they’re easy to pack in your luggage and pair with a bunch of ensembles.

Since 2022, we’ve tested over 25 travel blazers, seeing how they hold up in overhead bins, on sweaty commutes, and straight out of a bag. The best ones are tailored, not restrictive, lightweight but not flimsy, and polished without feeling overdone. No one’s traveling in a three-piece suit anymore. Here are the best travel blazers to get you through it all.

In the past year, our style team has tested dozens of travel blazers for functionality and Relwen has it in spades. Right off the bat, we noticed that its cotton-spandex fabric feels super lightweight and comes with enough stretch to let you move beyond limitations. It leans more sport jacket with a four-button design and throat latch that allows you to button all the way up to your neck. There are also functional buttons on the sleeves, which look sharp rolled up. I’ve worn it in low 50s as well as high 70s, and found it to be comfortable in both temps.

Normally, I have to pay to dry clean most of my blazers, but this one can be tossed around my washing machine without falling apart. As for storage, the three exterior patch pockets are similar to any casual blazer, but the large interior pocket has a zip closure with a vertical opening for easy access. It is ideal for stashing valuables.

On top of being a solid choice for away seminars or long flights, this option is great for everyday wear. It looks great during cool evening strolls, dinner dates, and outdoor weddings. Sure, this blazer gets wrinkled easily, but it’s designed to give off a laid-back vibe, as if it’s been worn and broken in over time.

In Rhone’s vast assortment, the brand carries a travel blazer with a killer slim cut. It has a sporty vibe, but looks clean enough for meetings that aren’t too formal. The Flex-Knit fabric is breathable and moisture-wicking, which means you stay cool and the garment doesn’t become damp or develop unpleasant odors from sweat. The polyester material has plenty of stretch, so I never felt any restriction in the arm area when I grabbed my coffee or reached up to the high cabinet.

I’ve paired it with everything from a basic tee to an oxford shirt, and it looks great with just about anything in your wardrobe—a true testament to its versatility. Plus, the material is ultra-light, making it a comfortable pick to throw on. Unlike Relwen’s travel blazer, this one can’t go in the washer—you have to take a trip to the dry cleaners.

Eddie Bauer’s travel blazer is practically indestructible. The fabric is hardcore and can take a beating, thanks to the reinforced seams and durable water-repellent finish. The latter especially makes sure you’re covered if you spill a drink or get caught in a downpour. And when you’re commuting, you can secure your passport or phone inside zippered compartments.

During our testing, we found that the two-way stretch made a journey a breeze, giving us the freedom to move through busy airports and crowded streets. Plus, the universal fit hits the sweet spot, so it’s comfortable for all body types without being too tight or too loose.

Although Uniqlo’s design looks like a wool blazer replica, it’s one of the most breathable styles I’ve ever worn. It’s made with the brand’s proprietary AirSense fabric, a lightweight polyester material that dries in minutes and keeps me cool. Typically, when I wear a traditional blazer in the summertime and in the muggy subway, I sweat like a dog. But when I wore this one in 80-degree weather to a work brunch, I was comfortable and dry the whole time. It’s relaxed enough to wear with chinos or jeans, but still has a dressy vibe that can pull off a full-suit look with trousers.

I found it’s not too fitted in the waist, which lets me layer shirts or knits easier in the cooler temps. There’s no bunching to where I feel stuffed. You can snag it in the typical neutral colors like gray and navy, perfect for the office followed by dinner plans. Like Relwen’s offering, this one is machine washable, but I recommend turning it inside out in a mesh bag. On the other hand, it’s way more structured with a natural shaping in the shoulders and sleeves. And yeah, it’s the most affordable option on this list, clocking in under $100, but it doesn’t look or feel like a budget buy. You’re getting the same premium quality that you’d get with a blazer that cost a few hundred bucks.

In an effort to max out comfort, Faherty offers a travel blazer made out of a stretch jersey knit fabric. It has a soft hand feel, tailored fit, and wears like your coziest cardigan. The front pockets are deep enough to carry your earbuds or wallet, so either won’t fall out as you’re maneuvering through the airport. Whether you’re packing it all in a backpack or suitcase, it’s a breeze to toss in and hit the road. Plus, we found no signs of wrinkles after unloading our clothes in the hotel.

Unlike stiff travel blazers that we’ve tested, this one bends and moves with you, so it doesn’t feel like you’re stuck in a straightjacket. The slimmer cut is perfect for guys who have an athletic or lean build, as it accentuates a trim silhouette and creates a sharp appearance. It’s a perfect match with a pair of summer pants, but looks just as cool with jeans and a tee.

When you want to look like you mean business at client dinners or conferences, you should reach for this blazer from Hugo Boss. Most travel blazers prioritize comfort at the expense of polish, but this one manages to deliver both. Our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan loves how sharp this slim-fit silhouette looks on him. He says it's tailored without feeling restrictive, while the stretch-infused, polyester-wool fabric gives you enough mobility for long flights and days spent hauling luggage through airports. The biggest differentiator, though, is right in the name: it’s washable. I can wear it repeatedly on a multi-day trip, freshen it up without a costly dry-cleaning bill, and pack it with far less anxiety than a traditional wool sport coat.

I wore the jacket on a full travel day that included a flight, a lengthy commute, and several hours seated at meetings. It kept its shape surprisingly well, resisting the creases and rumpling that typically throw off more formal tailoring after being folded inside a carry-on. What impressed me most was how effortlessly it transitioned from travel wear to evening attire. I could step off a plane and head directly to a dinner reservation without feeling underdressed. Admittedly, the jacket isn’t as soft or unstructured as more casual travel blazers from performance-focused brands. Also, the slimmer cut may feel less forgiving if you prefer a relaxed fit. But if your priority is maintaining a clean, business-ready vibe while still getting travel-friendly performance, I haven’t found many options that strike the balance as well as this one.

If you’re looking for a travel blazer that leans more dressy with European tailoring and luxurious quality for a great price point, Suitsupply is your best bet. Instead of a boxy, rigid silhouette that’s on trend right now, this timeless design has a natural shoulder, single-breasted closure, and a half-canvas construction that helps the jacket mold to your body over time while maintaining a solid drape.

It’s made with medium weight pure wool, but I wasn’t burning up wearing it with a tank top at a rooftop party. When the temperature really spikes beyond 80 degrees, I would recommend reaching for something lighter like linen. The chest and waist is trimmed for a slim fit, but it’s not too tight in the arms. I wore a 36R and didn’t need any alteration. It looks sharp straight off the rack. Sure, it’s on the pricier end compared to other picks on the list, but you’ll have this blazer for seasons to come. You can wear it to the office, formal business events, or weddings.

Linen blazers, like this one by Charles Tyrwhitt, reign supreme for travel because I stay cool, dry, and comfortable. As I’m commuting, airflow is constant, and it never feels stuffy like wool, even when the temps spike. Linen is notorious for wrinkling, but this one’s got enough structure that creases barely register—and the taupe color blends in, helping to mask any wrinkles that do show up.

The cut is relaxed through the chest and waist, with a clean, structured drape that follows the body without pulling. The shoulders are lightly structured, giving you shape up top without feeling stiff. It’s a sharper silhouette overall, but still works for guys with broader shoulders or a bigger chest. But if you’re on the leaner side, it captures that close-to-the-body, tailored look.

If you want a blazer that feels like a step up from your usual travel uniform, I would highly consider this number from Bonobos. Unlike stiff, restrictive blazers that make you feel like you’re trapped in a straightjacket, this cotton-spandex blend flexes with you, whether you’re reaching for your luggage in the overhead bin or hailing a cab. I have to admit, it does wrinkle quite a bit when I’m sitting down for a long amount of time. In true Bonobos fashion, this blazer comes in three fits—slim, athletic, and standard—so every guy can find his perfect match. And it’s far more relaxed than a traditional sport coat. Just a note: you can only take it to the dry cleaners. In terms of styling, it’s super versatile: you can wear it with a dress shirt and chinos for a garden party or a casual T-shirt and jeans for a laid-back look on your next trip.
