If I’m traveling somewhere warm and still want to look put-together, Buck Mason’s carry-on blazer is the one I keep coming back to. Its cotton-linen blend combines the breathability of pure linen along with the durability and structure of cotton. You get that relaxed, cool texture that makes linen so comfortable in the summer, but without the excessive wrinkling that can make traditional linen jackets look disheveled halfway through a trip.

What I liked most was how well it handled repeated packing and unpacking. While it picked up some natural creasing—as any linen-rich garment will—it never looked sloppy. The cotton component helped the jacket retain its shape, while the linen kept it noticeably cooler than traditional wool tailoring during warm afternoons. At 5’8”, I also appreciated that the silhouette felt tailored without being overly structured or stiff. The jacket’s biggest strength is versatility. It pairs just as naturally with chinos and loafers for a dinner reservation as it does with shorts and minimal sneakers for a day of sightseeing.

Unlike performance travel blazers that can sometimes look overly technical, the Capitola leans into classic menswear styling with a fabric that develops character the more you wear it. It’s not the blazer I’d choose for highly formal business settings, but for warm-weather travel, it’s one of the most wearable options I’ve tested.

When shopping for men’s travel blazers, look for fabrics that are comfy and practical. Men’s travel blazers are built to look like traditional blazers, while providing the feel and function of athletic outerwear. Go for stretchy materials like spandex or elastane, so you can move without any hassle or restriction. Wrinkle-resistant materials like polyester or blends are great because they remain looking sharp after you unravel them from your suitcase. Breathable materials like cotton and lightweight wool keep you cool and comfortable.

Make sure your blazer fits well and is comfortable enough to wear all day. Travel blazers for men should allow freedom of movement and not feel too tight or restrictive. The shoulders of the garment need to align with your own and not sag or pinch, as this affects the overall look. Always double-check the sleeves; see that they’re not too long and the armholes are high enough to avoid bunching while allowing mobility. When it comes to travel blazers, you'll typically find these three main types of fits.

A more tailored cut that's snug around the chest and waist, giving you a sharp, sleek silhouette. Great for guys who want a more fitted look without sacrificing comfort.

A fit that's perfect for guys with broader shoulders and a smaller waist. It offers more room in the chest and shoulders, while still tapering at the waist for a streamlined look.

The classic, relaxed fit. It offers more room throughout the body and is great for a laid-back, comfortable look. Ideal for guys who prioritize freedom of movement and a less structured feel.

A packable travel blazer can easily be folded or rolled up if it's taking too much space in your luggage, leaving room for other essentials. Having one that packs well means you can just throw it in the bag and go, making your travel preparations simpler and more efficient.

Check for practical features like multiple pockets for easy access to essentials and moisture-wicking properties if you intend to be active.

To find the best travel blazers for men, our style team led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, tested dozens over the past few years. We wore them during business conferences, day trips, and leisure vacations. We tested each one, checking to see which allowed for easy movement, felt light, and fit nicely throughout the body. We also analyzed the packing process and styled the blazer with different outfits to make sure it worked for both casual and formal settings. We then narrowed down to the eight best travel blazers for men that give you a stylish and refined look that attracts only the best kind of attention.

Think of your travel blazer more like a lightweight jacket. Any blazer in a dark, neutral color or simple pattern can go on top of pretty much any outfit. Whether you wear a button-down shirt or a hoodie, throwing a blazer over it instantly levels up your look. Alas, we tend to not use the pockets of suits or formal blazers very often, but you should utilize all the pocket space of travel blazers.

#4663. Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes at 50% off used

Once America’s most popular electric pickup, the Ford F-150 Lightning is finding a second life on the used market.

The F-150 Lightning is hard to pass up at 50% to 60% off sticker price, even used. With new models no longer available, Ford’s electric pickup is suddenly selling like hotcakes on the used market.

After the last model rolled off the assembly line last December, CEO Jim Farley said the decision to end production came as the “very high-end EVs, the $50K, 70K, $80,000 vehicles, they just weren’t selling.”

At 50% to 60% off, it now looks like a bargain in the used market. “When Ford was selling it brand new, the math was complicated,” Jimmy Douglas, CEO of Plug, a wholesale EV dealer, recently told Bloomberg.

On the used market, however, “the Lightning is 50% to 60% of the sticker price and that is really a sweet spot,” he added.

Used Ford F-150 Lightnings are selling in about 20 days, less than half the 44-day average for used vehicles in the US. According to Edmunds.com, prices are now up 4% to about $50,000 since the start of the year.

Douglass said that close to one-third of used models are sold by rival dealerships that would normally flip them back to Ford. However, many are opting to sell them directly because of demand.

Chase Norris from Colorado called the electric pickup a bargain. He purchased a used Lightning for around $40,000 and considers it a major upgrade from his previous gas F-150.

EV Group CEO and cofounder Alex Lawrence, which sells pre-owned electric vehicles, said he can’t get his hands on any reasonably priced used F-150 Lightnings currently.

He said many Lightning buyers use it as a second truck to save money during their weekly commute.

It looks essentially the same as the gas-powered F-150, offers instant torque, and produces zero tailpipe emissions, but the electric pickup failed to meet Ford’s expectations because of its higher price.

The base F-150 Lightning Pro debuted in 2021 with a starting MSRP of $39,974, but that was quickly raised to around $60,000 a year or so later.

According to Edmunds.com, the average transaction price for the F-150 Lightning in its first year of sales was $79,000 because Ford focused on higher-priced trims. The gas version’s ATP was about $19,000 less.

Even with the higher sticker price, Ford was losing a considerable amount on each Lightning it produced. In Q1 2024, Ford lost more than $100,000 on every EV it built.

Next year, Ford will take another crack at the electric pickup market with the Fathom, the first vehicle based on its “groundbreaking” new Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform.

Ford said the Fathom will start at $28,350 for the standard-range version. Even with the $1,595 delivery fee included, the electric pickup will start at under $30,000.

As the first vehicle built on its UEV platform, Ford promises the Fathom will be a step-change from its first-generation EVs.

According to Ford, the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4 and will be the first vehicle with Apple Maps directly integrated into the navigation system.

We also know the electric pickup will have a NACS port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger this summer.

Ford reportedly aims to sell around 100,000 Fathoms in its first year. CEO Jim Farley said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week that the launch remains on track for Q4 2027.

Farley called the Fathom a “breakthrough product” and said that the MSRP under $30,000 is perfect for today’s market.

At least some F-150 owners are already trading in for lower-priced options. A member of the Ford F-150 Lightning Owners Group, JF, said that although it was a great ride, “Carvana gave us just a little less than we paid new,” adding, “R2, here we come!”

When Torque News reached out, JF said he “really liked the Lightning,” but wanted something smaller. “With the current increase in resale value, the time to trade seemed right,” JF added.

The Rivian R2 (see our review) Performance with the Launch Package is now available to order starting at $57,990 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 330 miles and 656 hp. The R2 Premium will go on sale later this year, starting at $53,990

In Spring 2027, Rivian will launch the R2 Standard, starting at $44,990 with an estimated range of up to 275 miles and 350 hp.

So were they losing $100k / truck, or the average loss when all development was included ended up being $100k? Big difference. I don't believe the cost to build each one was $170k+. That makes no sense. They just priced them too high to amortize the development costs over enough vehicles to make them profitable. Every vehicle has to sell a minimum # before they start to make a profit.

Surging F-150 Lightning sales on the used market show buyers want electric pickups. But at the right price.

At $60,000 to $70,000, the Lightning wasn’t so attractive, but at $40,000 used, it suddenly is. Perhaps Ford is on to something with its next-gen EV pickup, the Fathom, set to go on sale starting at under $30,000.

Will it deliver on its promise? Ford has yet to reveal battery specs, towing capacity, range, or any other specs. We should learn more soon.

#4662. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.

#4661. E-quipment highlight: Jungheinrich launches new forklift for Asian markets

Like many equipment brands, German forklift maker Jungheinrich has been struggling to crack the Asian industrial markets – but the company is set to change all that with the launch of a new line of 1.6- to 3-ton class electric forklifts designed specifically to navigate the region’s tight warehouses and factories.

Jungheinrich launched the next generation of its EFG MB and MC electric counterbalance forklifts, giving businesses more flexibility to match truck performance with the battery options, charging systems, and operator features that meet their specific needs.

“Different operations have different requirements,” said Lisa Jing Xue, Managing Director at Jungheinrich’s Qingpu Plant, China. “With the EFG M series, customers can configure the (forklift) truck around their application, workload and operators – whether they need greater maneuverability for confined warehouse spaces, or a stable, powerful truck for demanding transport and stacking work.”

Forklift buyers can choose between two performance packages, prioritizing energy efficiency for everyday material handling or more driving and lifting muscle for more demanding, high-throughput operations. The higher-performance package comes standard on models rated for 2.5-3.0 tons, with a choice of either lead-acid or lithium-ion batteries with 346 or 690 Ah of capacity available to suit different workloads and shift patterns. Both ship with regenerative braking tech that can recover up to 30% of the energy used in stopping and lowering loads, too, helping to keep these machines running longer between charging sessions.

“We carried out extensive customer research to understand what the market needs,” added Jing Xue. “Customers can invest in the performance required today and add further capabilities as their application demands.”

Optional features include fingertip controls, a larger 4″ digital display, upgraded LED lighting, and operator-assistance (ADAS) systems, while flexible seating and cabin configurations are designed to keep drivers comfortable through long shifts. A slim B-pillar and glass roof help visibility in busy warehouses, while the four-wheel EFG MC gets automatic cornering speed reduction as standard. Integrated telematics are also standard, giving fleet managers access to utilization data, maintenance planning and pre-operational checks from day one.

Jungheinrich says the order books for both the three- and four-wheel electric forklifts are open now, ready to be supported by the company’s 6,000+ person strong service network across the Asia-Pacific region.

#4660. Three Key Behaviors of Highly Creative People

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

It may well be one of the most frequently asked questions by people from a wide range of occupations: “What do I need to do in order to become more creative?” Suffice it to say that there are several intertwining characteristics of those deemed to be innovative and imaginative. But, for our purposes, let’s take a look at three of the most-cited and most-recommended behaviors that positively influence our creative expression.

Curiosity is ingrained in our DNA. The mysteries of the universe have always been an impetus for us to peek and poke and prod for

answers - learning something new about our surroundings as well as about ourselves. We want to know more than we know; we want to expand our horizons, try out the new and undiscovered, and pursue experiences that deepen our comprehension (and appreciation) of the world in which we live.

But curiosity is much more than a simple search for answers. It is also the generation of possibilities. When we look at the world from multiple perspectives, we give ourselves permission to examine a wider range of resolutions and remedies. We open up our minds to explore the unexamined and unknown. Curiosity becomes a propellant for new opportunities and new options. Ian Leslie explains it this way: “…curiosity is essential to an exploring mind; it opens our eyes to the new and undiscovered, encouraging us to seek out new experiences and meet new people.”

It was Albert Einstein who famously said, “I have no special talents. I am only passionately curious.” For Einstein, curiosity was the engine that drove his creativity. Curiosity was his catalyst for questioning, and questioning is what propels us to seek out the unfamiliar and the unknown. For, without curiosity, knowledge becomes stagnant and immovable. It does not move us forward, nor does it have sufficient power to examine what may lie just beyond our experiences.

In conducting research for my latest book (see below), I came across some compelling insights underscoring the fact that creative thinkers tend to ask more open-ended questions. For example, a 2023 study in the Journal of Creativity took a look at the types of questions posed by 165 undergraduate students during select creative-thinking tasks. Individuals whose responses showed greater originality and fluency tended to ask more open-ended questions. The researchers also discovered that questions involving possibilities (rather than absolutes) were associated with originality in various tasks.

Consider the difference between these two questions: “Is this a good idea?” (This type of query invites a yes-no response. As such, it encourages evaluation before any exploration takes place.) and “What are some different ways this particular idea could be improved?” (This type of question, on the other hand, invites alternatives, experimentation, and the possibility of multiple solutions.) Additionally, there is evidence to indicate that open-ended questions may support creativity through several inter-related processes:

Perhaps most compelling are the open-ended questions we ask ourselves. These inwardly-directed queries often shape what we pay attention to, which alternatives we may conjure, and how we interpret our experiences. They give us a framework to muse, ponder, and think in several different directions. For example, contemplate these possibilities: “What could I learn that would help me improve?” “What did this attempt teach me, and what could I try next?” “What are six possible solutions, including unconventional ones?” and “What other approaches might work just as well – or better?” Note that these examples illustrate divergent ways of thinking – contemplations of what might be rather than what is. Or, in the words of Eugene Jonesco, “It is not the answer that enlightens, but the question.”

Taking risks is essential in our overall growth and development. We all took some risks when we learned how to walk. By the same token, we took a risk when we got our driver’s license and took the family car out for a spin, and many of us took a risk when we joined up with another individual and said that we would spend the rest of our lives with that person. Basically, taking risks is an essential element of our learning curve. Yet, what we often practice in the real world may be altogether different—minimize the risk, and you can minimize the potential defeats. But what results is often stunted creative expression. Innovation is all about taking a chance; all about venturing into unfamiliar territories with the possibility of discovering something new or something different. That’s not possible without risk-taking.

Creative individuals are known for taking chances. They examine the unknown – not necessarily because it will lead to something successful but rather because it’s new (Cue Leonardo da Vinci, Marie Curie, Pablo Picasso and Steve Jobs). Those individuals were happy to move beyond what they knew in order to play with unexplored ideas. Most importantly, they often envisioned the inevitability of failure as a creative learning opportunity…a chance to regroup and refocus.

By and large, creativity involves the freedom to move into uncharted territories and unfamiliar vistas. As such, risk-taking is an essential element of the creative life simply because it gives us license to step outside our comfort zone, challenge how we think, and explore a plethora of possibilities. When we give ourselves permission to experiment (and make mistakes), we open a door to unexpected discoveries and innovative ideas. Or, as Erich Fromm so eloquently put it, “Creativity requires the courage to let go of certainties.”

What is most important – especially for those who wish to enhance their creative spirit – is to constantly pursue, refresh, and master the three attributes above. Every day!

Leslie, Ian. Curious: The Desire to Know and Why Your Future Depends on it. (New York: Basic Books, 2024).

Fredericks, Anthony D. The Ultimate Book of Questions for Families. (North Haven, CT: Independent, 2026).

Acar, S., Berthiaume, K., & Johnson, R. (2023). What kind of questions do creative people ask? Journal of Creativity, 33(3), 100062. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcre.2023.100062.

Pillay, Srini. “A Better Way to Think About Risk.” Harvard Business Review. (December 23, 2014).

And of course, beyond their performance specs, these workout clothes just look great. It's not just about staying dry; it's also about the satisfaction of feeling good while breaking a sweat. That's why a workout shirt must seamlessly combine comfort, performance, and aesthetics to perfection.

All with that old school UA logo. Being tag-less with a straight hem, the fit is quite striking as well. And you get all of that with a minimal dent in the bank account.

Cotton may be the most dependable fabric for regular every-day t-shirts, but cotton holds onto moisture, which makes it a sweat trap, weighing you down. Instead, opt for synthetic, moisture-wicking fabrics like polyester and nylon that are lighter. They can also be woven in special ways that cotton can't be to enhance breathability. Synthetic fibers don't bleed and are hard to discolor, so they won't get sweat stains. Some menswear brands are even starting to use finely knit wool for its natural breathability, moisture wicking, and odor-fighting properties. Consider what feels best to you and in what environment you might be working out in.

In most clothing, seams are placed where they are easiest to construct the shirt or look the best. However, those places—like under your armpit and along the side of your body—are also high friction areas, especially when working out. Athletic brands have designed t-shirts that minimize the amount of seams and place them in areas that wont be impacted by your movement. Look out for seams and other high-contact areas that could prose a problem, depending on where they're located.

Simply put, your workout clothes get stinky when they hold on to sweat. A whole range of innovations exist that brands claim will fight odor, but the only sure fire way to keep your workout shirts from stinking are to keep them dry and wash them after every use. That means the workout shirts that retain the least amount of sweat are the easiest to keep from stinking. So if odor is a concern for you (as it should be), look for the shirts that dry the fastest and breath the best. There's a lot of new tech out now that helps combat stink.

Forward thinking labels are adding UV protection to workout clothes. Sunscreen is great, but even the best sweat-proof kinds can wear off during long and intense outdoor exercises. Not so with UPF clothing, which block UV rays to keep you protected during your entire sweat session, no reapplication necessary. Even the Skin Cancer Foundation has touted the skin-saving benefits of UPF clothing. If you're looking for even more sun protection, look for long-sleeve t-shirts, or hooded tops with UPF features.

Synthetic fabrics work especially well in workout shirts, as they're designed to handle moisture better than traditional materials. These fabrics include: polyester, Gore-Tex, nylon, and spandex, which have tiny spaces in knit or mesh that allow moisture to move through, evaporating quickly.

According to Dr. Corey L. Hartman, MD, an assistant clinical professor of dermatology at the University of Alabama School of Medicine, moisture-wicking fabrics help moisture from the inner layer of the fabric (the part that touches your skin) escape to the outside of the garment.

"Synthetic materials are better at moisture-wicking as they not only pull sweat moisture away from the skin, but they also dry quickly and don’t hold onto moisture," explains. Dr. Marisa Garshick, board-certified dermatologist of MDCS Dermatology.

"Cotton, on the other hand, while it can absorb sweat and moisture from the skin, it is more likely to hold onto the moisture and not dry as quickly, leaving the sweat in prolonged contact with the skin," she explains. Although, some cotton fabrics may be specially treated to make them moisture wicking.

Double checking the tags on your tops, or reading about the materials it's made of will help you pick proper shirts for your workouts. And thankfully, you can find moisture-wicking materials in tanks, short sleeve tees, long sleeve tees and hoodies.

So, why buy a workout shirt anyway? We've all worked out out in a regular cotton t-shirt at one time or another, and while it certainly won't ruin your gym session, it won't make it more enjoyable either.

The result of wearing shirts designed for athletic performance is that the fabric from which they're made feels drier and cooler against the skin.

"Moisture-wicking [shirts] can be especially beneficial when the body is subject to higher temperatures, like during a workout or a hot summer day," Dr. Hartman explains. Plus, keeping things cool and dry under your shirt can actually minimize a slew of issues.

"Buildup of sweat can lead to irritation which can appear as red, flaky patches or breakouts, which appear as red papules or pustules that may involve the hair follicle," explains Dr. Garshick.

There are some body odor perks, too (or lack thereof), according to Dr. Hartman. "Body odor occurs when sweat mixes with natural bacteria found on the skin. The less sweat on the skin, the less body odor."

#4658. Janus Electric secures battery supply deal for its battery-swap semi truck

Australian conversion specialists Janus Electric have been celebrating a growing slate of orders for their Class 8 electric truck conversions, which ditch diesel in favor of advanced battery-swap electric power – but exactly how they’d deliver all those trucks was still a question. Now, we have an answer: Electrovaya will supply the batteries.

The concept of dropping an electric power unit into a Class 8 semi makes perfect sense, as most of these trucks are built as gliders. That is, rolling body and chassis without an engine and transmission that’s ready to receive power from Cummins, Detroit, International, or Volvo Penta. That’s the role that Janus Electric sees itself occupying, and it seems to be working.

Janus’ reservation book crept past 70 units this past summer, helped along in part by California’s HVIP Program and the US EPA’s Diesel Emission Reduction Act (DERA) Grants. When the HVIP voucher is combined with the Port of Los Angeles’ “Plus” support, customers can received up to $166,000 per truck conversion. Factor in the massive fuel savings of electric and the classic good looks of square-nose Western Star truck body, and it’s easy to see why they’d be a popular choice.

As Jerry Seinfeld taught us however, it’s one thing to take a reservation – it’s another thing to deliver. To help make it happen, Janus has inked a battery supply deal with Electrovaya that will see a $26 million initial purchase orders for Electrovaya battery packs to demand for Janus’ products in the US and Canada, along with the battery company purchasing approximately $1.4 million in Janus stock with (what seems to be) actual money.

“Electrovaya is an important partner to Janus Electric, and we’re particularly pleased it has decided to invest directly in our business,” explains Ben Hutt, Managing Director and CEO of Janus Electric. “The investment is a strong vote of confidence in our technology and approach to electrifying heavy transport.”

The Janus Electric-repowered trucks carry a stout, 480 hp electric motor drawing power from a standard 310 kWh battery pack, with up to two battery packs (one on each side) of the truck. In practice, that gives the Janus trucks up to 370 miles of loaded range. After that, the batteries can be DC fast charged in under 90 minutes, or swapped for fresh ones in about four minutes without too much in the way of specialized equipment. That’s not just Janus’ killer app, it means that a battery supply deal like this one with a strategic partner who’s invested in the fledgling company’s success is such a huge deal.

“Reliable battery supply is critical to our growth,” adds Hutt, “and Electrovaya’s expanding North American manufacturing capabilities will be important as we scale. Both companies see considerable opportunity in this market, and we look forward to building on our partnership.”

For their part, Electrovoya executives seem to know their role here, and seem excited to be a part of what Janus is doing. “Class 8 trucking is one of the most exciting and demanding frontiers in electrification, and Janus has demonstrated real commercial traction with fleets in the US, Canada and Australia,” said Dr. Raj Das Gupta, CEO of Electrovaya. “Janus has developed a practical solution to one of the major challenges facing heavy transport, enabling diesel-powered trucks to be converted to electric without compromising their commercial operations.”

Electrovaya will be expanding its American manufacturing capacity with lithium-ion cell, module, and battery pack production at its new, potentially BABA-compliant facility in Jamestown, New York, which is expected to come online in 2027.

#4657. Childhood Trauma and Grief: Lessons From Batman and Two-Face

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The difference between a heroic caped crusader and a criminal mastermind may come down to who was waiting in the doorway after a very bad childhood.

Harvey Dent (Two-Face) and Bruce Wayne (Batman) both carry the weight of living losses: grief from a traumatic childhood that never fully ends. Bruce becomes Gotham’s protector, while Harvey becomes Two-Face, a sadistic supervillain who mirrors the abuse he internalized as a child. Their stories show how loss is shaped by the context in which it occurs.

We usually think of grief as something that follows a death, but some of the deepest grief comes from what never was, such as a safe, loving, and reliable family. Grief researchers call this nonfinite loss, or living loss. It is re-experienced throughout life and keeps demanding adjustment.1

In "The Dark Knight," Harvey is a driven, idealistic district attorney who becomes Two-Face after violence takes the woman he loves.2 The comics reveal an earlier story: a father who abused him, with outcomes decided by the flip of a coin.3,4 Long before that night, Harvey had lost security, trust, innocence, and a sense of his own authenticity. These are intangible losses, which are symbolic, invisible, more existential, and easy to bury under professional achievements.

His story is also less rare and outlandish than it seems. The World Health Organization estimates that about six in ten adults in North America and four in ten in Europe have had at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE).5 ACEs are correlated with increased risks of being involved in the criminal justice system, health-harming behaviours, poor psychological health, and poverty or homelessness, and higher mortality rates, in addition to chronic illnesses.

Early relationships teach us how to regulate ourselves and what to expect from the world.6 When caregivers become a source of threat, a child adapts. Parts of our psyche hide, go numb, or freeze. Freeze is a psychobiological conservation strategy that results in having fractured developmental egoic states; we adapt by hiding, repressing, or emotionally isolating certain aspects of ourselves, analogous to how we have been made to feel by others.7

Jungian analyst Donald Kalsched describes how a traumatized psyche will survive in pieces when it is not safe to be whole.8 Two-Face is what happens when that adaptation becomes literal and hardens into identity: a polarized psyche, split between idealism and rage. He demonstrates how unexpressed grief does not disappear, and how traumatic loss can tear us apart from the inside.

Bruce has his own devastating losses.9 The difference is Alfred, a secure attachment figure who is consistent, attuned, and present when it matters. With Alfred, Bruce could grieve beside someone instead of alone, and being able to access the right support allowed Bruce to engage in his grief in a more integrative way than Harvey.

While Bruce nonetheless demonstrates his own childhood attachment injury from the death of his parents, his relationship with his parents is portrayed as positive in the Batman films and comics. This highlights how Bruce had internalized what it means to be protected, co-regulated with when distressed, and supported by loving attachment figures in expressing his own autonomy or interdependence at a young age.

This illuminates how loss experiences are always shaped by the various relational contexts in which they occur. In practice, that means finding our own Alfred, as we all need a trusted and caring person who can help us tend old losses. It also means cultivating an inner Alfred within our own imagination—a steady, compassionate aspect of ourselves that helps us stay grounded when the pain surfaces, even when it is not possible to find such a person externally to us.

This piece draws on my book chapter, Shadows in Context: Two-Face, Batman, and Losses Associated with a Traumatic Childhood in Superhero Grief and the Multiverse of Loss: Considerations and Case Studies edited by Jill Harrington and Darcy Harris (2026), which is a new collection published by Routledge that uses superheroes and the multiverse to explore the impact of non-death loss on our psychology.10

2. Nolan, C. (Director). (2008). The Dark Knight [Film]. Warner Bros Pictures.

4. DeMatteis, J. M. (1995). Batman, Two-Face: Crime and Punishment. DC Comics.

5. World Health Organization. (2023). Tackling adverse childhood experiences (ACEs): State of the art and options for action. https://phwwhocc.co.uk/resources/tackling-adverse-childhood-experiences…

6. Shelvock, M. (2022). Understanding loss: Grief and attachment theory. Psychology Today.

7. Shelvock, M., & Bayly-Bruneel, A. (2024). Understanding psychosis: A continuum of trauma, dissociation. Psychology Today.

8. Kalsched, D. (2020). Opening the closed heart: Affect-focused clinical work with the victims of early trauma. Journal of Analytical Psychology, 65(1), 136–152.

#4656. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — also carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4655. Energica rises from the ashes with plans for cheaper electric motorcycles

The Italian electric motorcycle maker, which ceased operations in 2024 after entering judicial liquidation, has announced a major revival under new international ownership. And while the Energica name is returning, the company behind it is going to look quite different this time around.

Perhaps the biggest change is where the motorcycles will actually be built.

Energica says motorcycle production is moving to Asia, while design, engineering, research and development, as well as responsibility for technical and quality standards, will remain in Italy. The new manufacturing setup is expected to significantly reduce production costs, allowing Energica to cut motorcycle prices by around 20% compared to its previous models.

That could be a big deal for a company whose motorcycles were widely praised for their performance and technology, but were also firmly positioned at the premium end of the market.

The revival comes after Energica was acquired by Energica Pte. Ltd., a Singapore-based company backed by international private investors. Importantly, much of the technological know-how isn’t disappearing overseas with the manufacturing. Energica says its core engineering and design leadership remains in Italy, including longtime CTO Giampiero Testoni and designer Paolo Imeni.

The first motorcycle to make its comeback will be the Energica Experia, the company’s adventure-oriented electric sport-tourer. After that, Energica plans to progressively restart production of the Ego, Eva Ribelle, and EsseEsse9, eventually bringing its entire previous lineup back to market.

At least initially, those motorcycles will use their existing platforms, which should help Energica get bikes rolling off the production line faster without having to develop and homologate entirely new machines. But upgrades are already planned, including a new battery and improvements to range, efficiency, performance, and reliability.

Energica is also specifically targeting Europe, the United States, and Australia as it rebuilds its dealer and service networks. Existing owners haven’t been forgotten either. The company says service has already resumed and spare-parts shipments have restarted to dealers in several countries.

For anyone who followed the electric motorcycle industry over the last decade, Energica’s disappearance was a particularly painful one. This wasn’t some startup with a couple of renderings and a dream. Energica built some of the highest-performance electric motorcycles on the road and spent four seasons supplying the motorcycles for the FIM MotoE World Cup, experience that helped develop its high-voltage and DC fast-charging technology.

Now the company gets something relatively rare in the motorcycle industry: a second chance.

And if moving production to Asia really can knock around 20% off Energica’s prices while retaining the Italian engineering that made the bikes special in the first place, Energica 2.0 might have a considerably better shot at turning great electric motorcycles into a sustainable business.

It seems like moving toward Asian manufacturing is all but inevitable here. It was the expensive European manufacturing of low-volume motorcycles that weighed so heavily on Energica’s balance sheets in the years up to their financial troubles, and so shifting production to countries with both the expertise and the cost benefits for motorcycle manufacturing simply makes sense.

Energica isn’t alone in discovering the economics of moving electric motorcycle production to Asia. Zero Motorcycles spent years manufacturing its bikes in California before beginning a major shift toward production in the Philippines in 2023, including both complete motorcycles and major subassemblies. Now the company works with multiple factories, including major manufacturers like Zongshen in China, to reduce production costs for its electric motorcycles while still maintaining the ‘designed in California’ marketing angle.

It’s too early to tell how the new strategy will play out for Energica, but the fact that the company is now following a more well-worn trail is a positive sign for those who have spent the last two years hoping for a revival.

#4654. Tesla to end Cybertruck production as sales stall at ~10% of plan

Tesla is ending Cybertruck production. CEO Elon Musk announced early Friday that the automaker will “wind down” the electric pickup at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of 2027, about three and a half years after the first deliveries.

Musk says it’s to make room for more Cybercab production. But Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck is short on buyers, and it sells at roughly a tenth of the 250,000 units a year Tesla built its line for.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

That’s all he said. Nothing yet on how long Tesla will keep selling inventory or what happens to parts and service for existing owners.

Tesla doesn’t break out Cybertruck deliveries. It lumps them into “Other Models,” along with the Model S, Model X, and now the Semi.

That bucket tells the story anyway. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3 2026, down 48% year-over-year and the lowest since Q2 2021. With Model S and Model X production over since April, we estimated that 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks.

That’s a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. Tesla planned the Cybertruck line for 250,000 units annually, and its latest shareholder letter still lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. So the truck is selling at about 12% of plan, and roughly a quarter of what’s actually installed.

The US numbers from Cox Automotive are worse. Cox estimates 3,519 Cybertruck sales in Q1 2026 and 3,744 in Q2, down from 14,416 in Q3 2024.

And not all of those were real customers. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, and Musk’s companies took 1,339 in total, about 19% of US registrations that quarter. If it wasn’t for Musk’s self-dealing, the Cybertruck would probably be dead already.

Tesla tried to fix demand. It launched a cheaper rear-wheel-drive version in 2025 and pulled it months later, then brought a cheaper dual-motor trim to customers this summer. And then it raised prices by $5,000 in August. The dual-motor now starts at $74,990.

The “make room” explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of factory floor, by Tesla’s own count, and the Cybertruck line is already running at about a quarter of its installed capacity. Most of it is sitting idle.

The Cybercab also isn’t at a volume where it’s fighting anyone for floor space. Texas had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October, and Tesla built a separate line for its “unboxed” manufacturing process.

If Tesla needs more Cybercab capacity down the road, it has the space. What it doesn’t want is to keep paying for a truck with its own stainless steel body, its own castings, and its own supply chain at 30,000 units a year.

Let’s call this what it is. Tesla isn’t ending the Cybertruck because the Cybercab needs room. It’s ending it because nobody’s buying it at anything close to the volume Tesla planned, and supporting a low-volume vehicle this unique is expensive.

I wouldn’t be surprised if Tesla lost a couple of billions on the Cybertruck experiment. Between R&D, pushing suppliers to produce 250,000 trucks per year, and deploying its own production line capable of 125,000 trucks per year, Tesla has invested billions. And with only ~70,000 trucks delivered in roughly 3 years, it probably never made any positive cash flow from the program.

They are just in-between growth phases. No need to panic just because they have discontinued three vehicles and the last successful vehicle they launched was the Model Y in early 2020.

The Cybercab line gives Musk a forward-looking reason to wrap a product failure in. Tesla did the same thing when it ended Model S and Model X production this year to free up Fremont for Optimus. It’s a lot easier to say “we need room for the future” than “this didn’t sell.”

We’ve said it many times: the Cybertruck is genuinely impressive to drive. Steer-by-wire and rear-wheel steering are real engineering, and nobody else has put them in a production pickup. But Tesla built a 250,000-unit factory for a polarizing $75,000+ truck that can’t be sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets. It just cancelled it for Australia and New Zealand two weeks ago. The math was never going to work.

It’s truly a sign of Tesla today. Musk used to talk about having a more traditional electric truck design if Cybertruck fails, but I doubt we will see that. Again, Elon is betting the house on autonomy.

#4653. How to Motivate Children for Success in School

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 17, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Parents in America and around the world agree on this: We want our children to succeed in school. Intense pressure for academic achievement now dominates the lives of many American families.

American students, however, are not doing well. Perhaps even more concerning, they seem to have less interest in learning. High school and college teachers across the country now assign less reading to their students, and students still complain that this is more than they can manage. Many American high school and college students no longer read books!

There are several possible causes for our children's loss of interest in learning, and different causes for different children. The impact of screens is certainly important. Children no longer have the attention span for reading. Instead, they are scrolling and watching short videos. They may even believe that, in this way, they are learning.

1. Express enthusiastic interest in your child’s interests, even if these are not the interests you would choose. Learning begins with interest. Children's instinctive interest and curiosity about the world are the starting point for their motivation and enjoyment of learning. As soon as children begin to talk, they are constantly asking questions, seeking information, and wanting to know “why.” Too often, in our understandable effort to help improve their skills, we neglect this essential aspect of children’s motivation.

Make note of moments of interest and talk with your children about what interests them. Ask questions. Do "research" together. Help them develop their interests into projects and goals.

The promise of rewards or the threat of punishment may lead to some short-term improvement in a child’s effort. But rewards and punishments cannot create interest, enjoyment, or long-term goals

2. Find the source of their anxiety, frustration, and discouragement. Parents often ask, "Why doesn’t he put more effort into his schoolwork? Why doesn’t he care?” The answer to these questions is almost always, “Because he is discouraged.”

Children may mask their discouragement with defiant or rebellious attitudes, and they may pretend that they don’t care. But they do care. If we look hard enough, we will find in every child some interest and a desire to do well.

Undiagnosed attention and learning disorders are a common source of discouragement and lack of sustained effort in children and adolescents. It is essential for parents and teachers to understand the impact of these difficulties. Even mild or moderate learning problems can be a source of anxiety, frustration, and low self-esteem.

3. Make note of every improvement, not every mistake. To solve the problem of discouragement, children need more encouragement and less criticism. Of course, to improve their skills, children need criticism. But they need encouragement even more. Encouragement is not false praise. We all need encouragement, even as adults, with every new challenge and skill we attempt to master.

4. Help them cultivate a growth mindset. Praise effort, not intelligence or talent. Praise learning, not grades. Then, on this foundation, we can set high standards and challenge children to work harder. But we will have to do this less often, because they will more often challenge themselves.

5. Appreciate their strengths. Students who seem unmotivated are often focused on their weaknesses, not on their strengths.

When I talk with “unmotivated” children, I often find qualities of intelligence, creativity, effort, and character that their parents and teachers have overlooked and that they may also fail to appreciate. When I point out these qualities, many children and adolescents feel deeply understood. For some, this is a transformative moment. Years later, these affirming statements are what they remember and value most about our work.

6. Make learning meaningful. Individual achievement alone—getting good grades in school—is a fragile source of motivation and effort, with a high cost in anxiety and stress. If we define achievement, however, as making a contribution to our families, our communities, our country, and the world, we offer children a much better goal and standard for success. We should help them become involved in projects that help their community, and we should be involved with them.

7. Have conversations. Every moment of dialogue with our children and grandchildren adds meaning and relevance to learning. Talk with your children about what they are studying—about civics and history, science, literature, and religion—and the importance of these subjects to our current lives. Talk with them about how others help us, about the good work that many people are doing, and what they can do to help others.

Conversation is a (partial) antidote to the addictive pull of screens. Before you ask, “Have you done your homework?” ask them about what they have been learning in school.

8. Establish "library hours" in your home. Even when children are highly motivated to do well in school, they still need to establish good work habits. They need to put away their devices, do their homework, and get enough sleep.

I encourage parents to set aside a specified time, early in the evening, as a homework or “library” hour. During the library hour, all electronics should be turned off (except for computers or tablets children need for schoolwork) for the entire family. No television, no video games, no phones.

Homework should be done in a communal place (as in a library), at the kitchen or dining room table. Especially with younger children, parents are present and available to help, offer encouragement, and answer questions. Then, when homework is done, there is time for play.

Most families have found these guidelines helpful for students of all ages. The result is an important lesson in self-discipline, fewer family arguments, and more success in school.

West, M. R. Student Test Scores Keep Falling. What's Really to Blame? Education Week, September 9, 2025.

Horowitch, J. The Elite College Students Who Can't Read Books. The Atlantic, October 1, 2024.

Engel, S. (2018). The Hungry Mind. The Origins of Curiosity in Childhood. Harvard University Press.

Dweck, C. (2007) Mindset: The New Psychology of Success (2nd Edition). Ballantine Books.

#4652. The 16 Best Undershirts for Men, Tested by Style Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Hanes and Mack Weldon came out on top in our testing.

A GREAT UNDERSHIRT is my first line of defense against sweat, stains, and overheating. It’s like the menswear equivalent of SPF. I learned that the hard way years ago, when I wore a flimsy cotton tee under a light-blue dress shirt to a summer wedding and, by cocktail hour, looked like I’d run a 10K instead of walked down the aisle. Never again. Now, if I’m layering under a dress shirt or sweater, I want something that works hard without me ever thinking about it. The best undershirts are so comfortable, I forget they’re even on. Unlike cheap, bulky options that ride up, trap heat, or lose their shape after a few washes, the real standouts are lightweight, moisture-wicking, and cut with a trim fit that stays put without squeezing the life out of you. They also tuck away neatly into trousers and save your other shirts from pit stains.

To find the GOATs, our fashion team and I tested more than 50 styles—everything from V-neck tees and tank tops to classic white crewnecks—wearing them under button-downs, sweaters, and even on their own. The winners disappear under your clothes like a good stunt double, regulate temperature like built-in AC, and keep you looking cool, calm, and collected from your morning commute to last call.

Hanes is perhaps the most famous undershirt brand on the planet. I’ve been wearing its undergarments since I was about 10 years old, and over the time, they've just become better in terms of fit and feel. For example, I’ve been wearing Hanes’ performance undershirt for four months, and it’s consistently comfortable, breathable, and snug in all the right places.

The shoulders sit perfectly without pulling, the chest drapes close without clinging, and the sleeves are tailored to follow your arms without cutting into your biceps. When an undershirt feels this light, I brace myself for it to be flimsy and tear like tissue, but it's impressively solid—and I didn’t even sweat in it. Unlike other undershirts that I’ve tested, this one has a structured collar and hem that keeps its shape. The polyester-rayon fabric is extra smooth and cool to the touch, even after wearing it for hours at the office. I also appreciate that the fabric blend is much lighter in weight than a traditional cotton undershirt.

After putting it through at least eight washes, I noticed that the fabric didn’t fade or shrink. One way I preserve it is by letting it air dry instead of tossing it in the dryer under high heat. It’s long enough to tuck in and doesn’t bunch under an overshirt. Since it's blended with a hint of stretch, I could grab a box off a high shelf without any restriction. Hanes uses the same double-needle stitching to reinforce the neck, sleeves, and hem as with their regular undershirts. This will stand up to years of washing and wearing with steady use. It only comes in white, but you can wear it with so many different fits—solo or layered.

Mack Weldon was founded to reinvent men's underwear and loungewear with better fabric blends and quality construction. Take its V-neck style undershirt that I've been wearing for a couple months now. It’s cut from a polyamide-elastane blend—the same kind of technical fabric in our favorite workout clothes. It’s got that silky-soft hand feel with real stretch baked in. I can lift my arms, reach overhead, and wrestle into a jacket on the subway, and I don’t feel any tugging in the arms. The neckline sits low enough to disappear when I don’t want it to be seen under my dress shirts, but not so deep it feels flimsy or overly delicate.

What really sold me, though, is the breathability. Even under my chunky sweaters with some heft, I never break a sweat or find myself needing to flap my knit like I'm trying to cool off. Since it has a slim fit, it sits close to my skin without being tight, but stays dry when I’m making my way through the muggy subway or sitting in non-air-conditioned areas at the office. I tossed it in the wash at least six times and the white still looks just as good as the day it came out the pack.

Tommy John V-neck undershirt is step above your average option when it comes to polished layering. Its slim cut and modal fabric give it shape and structure, so it skims the body without feeling tight—perfect for showing off a chest workout without clinging in an unflattering way.

One of the best features is how it tucks. The snug-but-not-tight fit keeps the shirt neatly in place under dress shirts or sweaters, so you don’t get bunching or riding up. This makes it ideal for formal and office-ready attire, where a clean, smooth base layer is essential. It’s also stretchy without being too thin and has yet to pill, five washes later. I recommend letting it air dry, so it doesn’t shrink or become tight since the undershirt has a slim fit.

After multiple wears, the V collar doesn’t give “bacon neck”, which makes it look worn-out. It sits closer to the neck than Mack Weldon’s version, but I still can hide it by closing the top two buttons of my dress shirt. I love the buttery-soft feel, which is breathable and light even in warmer 70-degree temps.

This is one of those cases where it's worth paying the extra bucks for an American-made garment.

The Made in America factor isn't just for show. The quality that comes with it is apparent. So if you ever need to shed a layer or two, you can fall back on this as a base layer t-shirt. You can even style it on a hot day with just a pair of shorts.

More importantly, we found that Jockey has nailed the standard 100% cotton plain white undershirt in the best way possible. It feels like a traditional soft cotton tee, but after putting it through the wash and dry cycles more than a dozen times, it managed to withstand all the wear and tear and stay intact, proving its durability. The fabric even has a tech built-in to reduce piling and fading. And I love that the cotton is engineered to be able to wick away sweat in a heartbeat to keep me fresh all day. The only thing is that the fabric isn't wrinkle-resistant, so store these shirts carefully.
